lessons.plain: A sustainability objective is a clear, checkable goal about reducing harm to the environment, treating people fairly, or keeping an organization or project viable over the long run. This lesson covers the why behind it: why a company or team decides to change how it works, and why one person chooses to commit personally. People rarely act for one reason. Some motives are about money or legal duty, some about reputation or customers, and some about values. A project manager who understands these motives can set goals that people actually support, and can explain to a sponsor why a goal is worth its cost.
lessons.guessPrompt: A construction firm wants its site trucks to burn less diesel. Name two different reasons the firm might care about this, and one reason a site engineer might personally care, even if nobody asked her to.
lessons.teach:
A sustainability objective is a specific goal, with a measure and a date, that aims to reduce environmental harm, improve outcomes for people, or keep a project or organization able to operate over time. An organization's reasons for adopting one are called its drivers. Common drivers include legal requirements such as emissions limits, cost savings from using less energy or fewer materials, pressure from customers, lenders or investors, the need to keep a license to operate in a community, and risk management, meaning protection against disruption such as flooding or supply shortages. Individual commitment usually comes from values, a sense of purpose, the expectations of one's team, or a personal stake such as living near a polluted site.

Why it works: a goal changes behavior only when the people doing the work see a reason that matters to them. Linking an objective to several drivers makes it more durable, because if one driver weakens, the others still hold.

Worked example: a site builder sets the objective 'cut diesel use by 25 percent against last year by the end of phase two.' Step one, the measure is litres of diesel per month, taken from fuel records. Step two, the baseline is last year's monthly figure. Step three, the date is the end of phase two. Step four, the drivers are fuel cost, a regional emissions permit, and a client contract clause. Step five, the site engineer commits because generator fumes affect a nearby school.

Common mistake: writing 'be more sustainable' and assuming everyone shares the same reason. A vague aim cannot be measured, and a single motive often fails when budgets tighten.

The project manager's job is to make the objective measurable, name the drivers behind it, and check that the people asked to deliver it can see why it matters to them.

questions.prompt: A regional water utility sets this objective: 'cut non-revenue water from 30 percent to 22 percent of total production by 31 March next year.' Non-revenue water means treated water that leaks away or is delivered but never billed. The steps are: (1) the measure is the monthly percentage of production lost, taken from meter reconciliation; (2) the date is 31 March next year; (3) [missing]; (4) the drivers are a regulator's loss limit, rising pumping costs, and a lender's loan covenant. Which entry correctly fills step three, the baseline, meaning the starting figure that progress is compared against?
choices: The pumping cost per megalitre, because cost is the main reason the utility acts
The number of leak-repair crews the utility has assigned to the distribution network
The 30 percent average of the prior twelve months, taken from the same meter records
The regulator's loss limit, since limits are always the starting point for any target
questions.why: A baseline is the starting measurement, and it must use the same measure and source as the target so that progress can be compared fairly.

questions.prompt: Which statement best matches how the course defines a sustainability objective?
choices: A legal permit that sets a maximum emissions level for one specific site
A broad promise to act responsibly across the whole organisation in future years
A dated, measurable goal aimed at less harm, better outcomes for people, or lasting operation
An annual report summarising how much the organisation spent on energy last year
questions.why: The course defines the objective as a specific goal with a measure and a date that targets environmental harm, people's outcomes, or continued operation.

questions.prompt: A distribution centre's only stated reason for its packaging-waste objective is a cost saving. When a supplier changes its price terms, the saving disappears and the team drops the work. Which response best follows the course's reasoning?
choices: Link the objective to further drivers, such as a customer contract clause, so that a weakening of one does not undo it
Raise the target sharply so the team works harder to offset the lost cost saving across all remaining months of the year
Remove the date from the objective so the goal can be pursued for longer without a deadline pressuring the team
Hide the supplier cost data from the team so that people focus only on the environmental side of the goal
questions.why: Linking an objective to several drivers makes it durable, because if one driver weakens the others still hold.

questions.prompt: A civil engineer on a road-building project says she personally wants dust controlled, even though the contract only requires it on paper. She lives two streets from the haul route, and her child has asthma. Which driver from the course best explains her commitment?
choices: Cost savings from fewer water tankers used for dust suppression on the haul route
A legal requirement that applies only to her as an individual rather than the firm
Lender pressure on the contractor's loan terms tied to dust-related reporting
A personal stake, because dust from the haul route affects her own household directly
questions.why: The course lists a personal stake, such as living near a harmful site, as a common source of individual commitment.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why an organization might adopt a sustainability objective and why an individual might commit to one. Name one limit or tradeoff of relying on each kind of motive.
lessons.modelAnswer: Organizations usually adopt sustainability objectives for a mix of drivers: legal duties such as emissions limits, cost savings from using less energy or material, pressure from customers and investors, keeping permission to operate from the local community, and reducing exposure to risks like flooding or supply shortages. Individuals commit for their own reasons: values, a sense of purpose, what their team expects, or a personal stake in the outcome. The limit of organizational motives is that they can weaken. If fuel prices fall or a rule is relaxed, the reason to keep going shrinks unless other drivers still apply. The limit of personal motives is that they depend on the person staying engaged and having the time and budget to act, so a project plan should not rest on one person's enthusiasm alone.
rubricPoints: Names at least two organizational drivers, such as legal duty, cost savings, stakeholder pressure, or risk reduction.
Names at least one individual motive, such as values, purpose, team norms, or personal stake.
States that an objective needs a measure, a baseline, and a date to be checkable.
Names a limit or tradeoff: an organizational driver can weaken, or personal commitment can fade.

suggested.rationale: Explaining these motives back to a teammate is the core skill here, and no existing mission or planned engine covers sustainability motives.

lessons.plain: The Triple Bottom Line is a way of judging a project by three kinds of results at once: how it affects people, how it affects the planet, and whether it creates lasting economic value. Think of a three-legged stool: if one leg is much shorter than the others, the stool wobbles. A project that makes a lot of money but harms workers or pollutes a river is not a good project under this lens, even if its accounts look healthy. The idea asks a project team to look for the costs and benefits that a normal budget would miss, and to balance them rather than maximise just one.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a city wants a new bus depot and the cheapest site is beside a wetland. Besides construction cost, what other effects would you want to weigh before choosing the site, and why might the cheapest site still be the wrong choice?
lessons.teach:
The Triple Bottom Line, usually shortened to TBL, is a framework that asks a project to weigh results in three areas. People covers the effect on humans: workers' safety and pay, the health of customers, and fairness to affected communities. Planet covers the effect on the natural environment: emissions, water use, land, wildlife, and waste. Prosperity covers economic viability: whole-life cost, revenue or savings, and the lasting economic value left in the place where the work happens. The framework matters because a normal project budget only records prosperity, so harms to people and planet stay invisible until they become expensive. Putting all three on the same table makes those hidden costs visible.

Worked example. A rural clinic runs diesel generators that break down often. A project proposes solar panels with a battery store. Step one, People: patients keep power during outages, and local technicians are trained to maintain the system. Step two, Planet: diesel burning and fuel deliveries stop, but the plan must include safe battery disposal at end of life. Step three, Prosperity: the upfront cost is higher, but fuel and repair savings over twenty years are larger, so whole-life cost falls. Step four: the team checks each area for weakness. Here the battery disposal plan is missing, so the project is not yet ready to approve.

Common mistake: treating the three areas as a checklist where each one gets a tick, instead of looking for trade-offs. A project can improve one area by damaging another, such as a cheap site that displaces a village. The consequence is that a project that looks profitable on paper gets stopped later by community opposition, regulators, or a failed audit, and that costs more than the savings it promised.

The Triple Bottom Line gives a project team a structured way to judge whether a choice is sound across people, planet, and prosperity together, rather than on economic terms alone.

questions.prompt: A regional school district plans to replace its three old gas boilers with air-source heat pumps. Work through the Triple Bottom Line for this project. Step one, People: students and staff keep heating during cold snaps, and facilities technicians are trained to service the new units. Step two, Planet: gas burning stops, and the plan confirms that refrigerant is handled safely at installation and disposal. Step three, Prosperity: [missing step]. Step four: the team checks each area for weakness. The project is ready to approve only if the step-three gap is filled.
choices: Compare whole-life cost, including the higher purchase price, lower running costs and repair costs over the system's life, and record any lasting economic value for the district.
Assume the savings are zero, because heat pumps are electric and therefore cost nothing to run.
Skip prosperity for this project, because a public school district is not a business and has no economic considerations.
Record only the purchase price, because the project budget is the only place where prosperity is measured.
questions.why: Prosperity covers whole-life cost and lasting economic value, so step three must compare the full cost picture over the system's life, not just the purchase price or a made-up figure.

questions.prompt: Which of the three Triple Bottom Line areas covers workers' pay, safety and the health of customers?
choices: Governance, because safety rules are set by management
Planet, because worker safety is a natural-environment concern
Prosperity, because pay is always an economic measure
People, because it covers the effect on humans including workers and customers
questions.why: People covers the effect on humans, which includes workers' safety and pay and customers' health.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm picks the cheapest site for a new warehouse. Its cost figures pass, and its planned rooftop solar array passes the environmental review. However, a wetland that local fishing families depend on for their income will be drained. Which Triple Bottom Line area is the team failing to weigh properly, and why does that matter?
choices: People, because the fishing families lose their livelihood, a harm a cost-only view would miss, and the project may be stopped later by opposition
Planet, because the solar array shows the environment has been checked
Prosperity, because the cost savings are already the main measure of the project
None of the areas, because a checklist that passes every item is always sound
questions.why: The People area covers fairness and livelihoods of affected communities, and ignoring that harm is the trade-off the framework is designed to expose.

questions.prompt: A bakery expansion scores well on prosperity, since the payback period is short, and on planet, since its ovens use less energy. The team has not reviewed worker safety for the new equipment. What is the correct conclusion under the Triple Bottom Line?
choices: The project is ready, because prosperity is the area that decides approval.
The project should be approved and the safety review done after the equipment is installed.
The project is not yet ready, because the People area has an unchecked gap and each area must be examined for weakness.
The project is ready, because two of the three areas are strong enough to outweigh the gap.
questions.why: The framework asks the team to check all three areas for weakness, so an unreviewed People area means the project is not yet ready to approve.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only managed budgets what the Triple Bottom Line is, using one example from your own work or a city project, and name one limit or trade-off of using it.
lessons.modelAnswer: The Triple Bottom Line asks us to judge a project on three results at once: People, meaning effects on workers, customers and nearby communities; Planet, meaning effects on emissions, water, land and waste; and Prosperity, meaning economic viability over the whole life of the work, including cost, savings and local economic value. For example, if we replace a city's old street lights with energy-efficient fittings, People covers safer lighting and any installer jobs, Planet covers lower electricity use and how the old lamps are recycled, and Prosperity covers the upfront price against years of energy savings. The main limit is that the three areas are hard to compare: there is no agreed exchange rate between a healthier community and a lower carbon figure, so the team has to make a judgement and record it openly. It is also easy to score the areas as separate tick-boxes, which hides the trade-offs. I would ask the team to name where the areas conflict before approving anything.
rubricPoints: Defines People, Planet and Prosperity accurately in everyday words.
Gives a concrete project example showing effects in all three areas.
Names a limit, such as the areas being hard to compare or weigh against each other.
Explains that the areas should be weighed together, not ticked off separately.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the three areas and their trade-offs back to a teammate is the core skill, and no listed mission or planned engine teaches this concept directly.

lessons.plain: Some sustainability work is measured against shared global lists rather than private rules. Two of the best known are the UN Sustainable Development Goals, a set of 17 worldwide goals for people, planet and prosperity agreed by world governments, and the UN Global Compact, a voluntary pledge that businesses make to follow ten principles on human rights, labour, environment and anti-corruption. Knowing which one a situation calls for is a first step. The goals describe what the world is trying to achieve, while the Compact describes how a company should behave while it works. An analogy: the goals are the destination on a map, and the Compact is the rulebook for the road you drive.
lessons.guessPrompt: A construction firm wants to show that its new bridge benefits the wider community, and also commit to fair labour practices across its suppliers. Which two global frameworks would you point to first, and why might they be different kinds of thing?
lessons.teach:
The UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are 17 goals adopted by UN member states in 2015 as part of a wider agenda, with 169 more specific targets underneath them. Each goal names a broad development aim, such as clean water and sanitation (Goal 6), decent work and economic growth (Goal 8), or climate action (Goal 13). They are aspirations for countries and the world as a whole, tracked through national indicators. A single company does not hold them as a licence.

The UN Global Compact is a voluntary initiative, launched in 2000, in which businesses commit to ten principles. The principles cover four areas: human rights (principles 1 and 2), labour (principles 3 to 6), environment (principles 7 to 9), and anti-corruption (principle 10). Participating companies report on their progress.

Why it works: the SDGs give many actors a shared target to line their work up against, and the Compact gives each company a concrete conduct standard to test its own operations against.

Worked example: a team builds a water treatment plant for a district. Step 1: the plant clearly advances SDG 6, clean water and sanitation. Step 2: the contractor's purchasing and site rules are checked against Global Compact labour and environment principles, such as no forced labour among suppliers and responsible handling of waste. Step 3: the project records both links so that later reporting can point to them.

Common mistake: calling a project 'SDG-aligned' because it sounds good, with no measurable link to a specific goal or target. Consequence: in a running programme, unsupported claims are the first thing auditors and investors challenge, and they weaken the credibility of later ESG disclosures.

The right frame is simple: name the goal for what the project achieves in the world, and name the Compact principle for how the organization conducts itself.

questions.prompt: Hollis Timber Works, a furniture maker, funds heat-recovery units on four drying kilns. The project is expected to cut its emissions by 320 tonnes of CO2 a year, which advances SDG 13, climate action. The team then writes a new supplier contract requiring that no workers at the timber supplier are forced to work or paid below the legal minimum. Step 1 is done: the project is linked to SDG 13. Step 2 is the supplier contract check. Which Global Compact area should that check be recorded against, so the company's conduct is tied to a named standard?
choices: SDG 13 again, because the contract also concerns climate
SDG 8 alone, since decent work is a development goal
The Global Compact labour principles (principles 3 to 6)
The Global Compact anti-corruption principle (principle 10)
questions.why: The worked idea is that the goal names what the project achieves in the world while a Compact principle names how the organisation conducts itself, and a supplier's labour conditions fall under the labour principles 3 to 6.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes the UN Sustainable Development Goals from the UN Global Compact?
choices: The SDGs are a voluntary company pledge with ten principles, and the Compact is 17 goals set in 2015.
The SDGs are 17 goals adopted by UN member states and tracked through national indicators, while the Compact is a voluntary initiative in which businesses commit to ten principles.
The Compact has 169 targets and the SDGs have ten principles that cover four areas.
Both are national laws that companies must report against each year.
questions.why: The SDGs are 17 goals with 169 targets adopted by states in 2015, while the Compact is a voluntary business initiative built on ten principles, so the third option separates them correctly.

questions.prompt: A bottling company says its new recycling line is 'SDG-aligned' because it sounds good to investors. What is the best correction to make before this claim appears in the ESG report?
choices: Drop the SDG reference and cite only the Global Compact, since it is the only framework that applies to companies.
Name the specific SDG and target the line advances, and record a measurable link such as tonnes of plastic diverted.
State that the line supports sustainability in general, which avoids the need for a specific link.
Replace the claim with a statement that the company is certified against the SDGs.
questions.why: A claim of alignment needs a specific goal or target and a measurable link, which is what the fourth option supplies, whereas the other options either overclaim or fall back on a generic statement.

questions.prompt: A regional haulage firm states that because it joined the UN Global Compact and publishes a progress report, it now holds the SDGs as a licence and has been certified as meeting them. Which response identifies the flaw?
choices: The firm is correct that the Compact reports count toward SDG certification once a year.
The firm's report is invalid because progress reports must be filed with national governments.
The firm should have joined the SDG initiative instead, because the Compact covers only anti-corruption.
The SDGs are aspirations tracked through national indicators and are not held by a single company, and the Compact is a voluntary commitment that does not certify anything.
questions.why: The SDGs are country-level aspirations that a single company does not hold as a licence, and the Compact is voluntary, so joining it and reporting progress does not amount to certification.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between the UN Sustainable Development Goals and the UN Global Compact, and name one limit or tradeoff of using either one as a project's only sustainability reference.
lessons.modelAnswer: The SDGs are 17 goals, adopted by UN member states in 2015, that describe development outcomes for countries and the world, such as clean water or decent work, each broken into specific targets. The UN Global Compact is a voluntary initiative for businesses, launched in 2000, built around ten principles on human rights, labour, environment and anti-corruption. So the goals say what we want to achieve in the world, and the Compact says how a company should conduct itself. The limit of relying on only one is clear. The SDGs cannot tell you how your supplier treats its workers, and the Compact does not say which social outcome your project delivers. Using the goals alone can produce vague claims of impact, and using the Compact alone can leave the project's benefits unmeasured. A good project names both.
rubricPoints: The SDGs are 17 UN goals for countries and the world, adopted in 2015, with targets beneath them.
The UN Global Compact is a voluntary business initiative built on ten principles across four areas.
The two frameworks answer different questions: outcomes achieved versus organizational conduct.
Using only one framework leaves a gap, such as unmeasured impact or unverified conduct.

suggested.rationale: This objective is recall of named frameworks and their structure, which is best learned from reference material, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it.

lessons.plain: Sustainability reporting is the practice of telling outsiders, such as investors, regulators, customers and communities, what a project or organization did about its environmental, social and governance effects, and how those effects affect its finances. ESG disclosures are the specific statements made about those topics. Several standard sets exist that say which facts to report and how to present them, so one company's report can be compared with another's. In a project, the project manager often supplies the data for these reports, so knowing which standard a report follows tells you what data to collect.
lessons.guessPrompt: A regulator asks a construction project to publish its carbon emissions in a form investors can compare with other builders' figures. Do you expect every company to choose its own layout, or would a shared set of rules and metrics be needed? Give your best guess and one reason for it.
lessons.teach:
ESG stands for Environmental, Social and Governance, which are three broad groups of factors such as emissions, workforce safety and board oversight. An ESG disclosure is a statement a company publishes about one or more of those factors. A disclosure standard is a rulebook that says what to report, how to measure it and how to present it. The main standards in this objective are GRI, SASB, TCFD and the IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards.

GRI (Global Reporting Initiative) asks an organization to report its impacts on the economy, the environment and people, and it is written for a wide range of stakeholders. SASB (Sustainability Accounting Standards Board) provides industry-specific metrics chosen for their likely effect on investor value; it now sits within the IFRS Foundation. TCFD (Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures) organized climate disclosure around governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets. Its work was carried forward by the ISSB (International Sustainability Standards Board), which issued IFRS S1 for general sustainability-related information and IFRS S2 for climate-related information.

Worked example: a road project in a flood-prone valley. First, the team identifies flooding as a climate risk. Second, it records who oversees that risk, how it changes the plan, and how the team manages it, which follows the TCFD structure. Third, it reports a metric such as expected days of delay, with a target for reducing them. Fourth, the same facts are shaped to meet IFRS S2 requirements for investors.

Common mistake: treating ESG and the frameworks as the same thing. ESG names the topics; a framework specifies the required content and format. A report can mention ESG topics without following any framework, which makes it hard to compare with other reports.

Consequence: if project data is collected without the chosen standard in mind, the team may find later that required metrics are missing and must gather them again, which delays the report. The standard you are asked to follow decides the data you must collect from the start.

questions.prompt: A regional rail operator is preparing its first sustainability report for local residents, unions and regulators. They want to know how the service affects local jobs, air quality and spending in towns along the line. The team has already listed the impacts to cover. Step 1: the team confirms the report is written for a wide audience, not only investors. Step 2: the team selects the disclosure standard that asks an organization to report its impacts on the economy, the environment and people. Step 3: the team gathers the data that standard calls for, such as jobs created and emissions per passenger-kilometre. What is the missing Step 2 standard?
choices: SASB, because it lists industry metrics chosen for their likely effect on investor value
GRI, because it asks for impacts on the economy, the environment and people and is written for many stakeholders
TCFD, because it organizes disclosure around governance, strategy, risk and metrics for climate
IFRS S2, because it is the standard for climate-related information aimed at investors
questions.why: GRI is the standard that asks for impacts on the economy, the environment and people, and it is written for a wide range of stakeholders, which matches this audience.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly separates ESG from a disclosure framework?
choices: A report that names ESG topics automatically meets GRI requirements
ESG names the broad factor groups such as emissions and board oversight, while a framework specifies what to report, how to measure it and how to present it
A framework is a list of topics such as emissions, while ESG is the rulebook for measuring them
ESG and the frameworks are the same thing, since both list the same topics
questions.why: ESG names the topic groups, and a framework is the rulebook that sets required content, measurement and presentation, so the two are different things.

questions.prompt: An industrial port operator's bond investors ask for a small set of metrics specific to port operations, chosen for how likely they are to affect the company's value. Which standard fits this request best?
choices: SASB, because it provides industry-specific metrics chosen for their likely effect on investor value
TCFD, because it sets metrics and targets for all sustainability topics across all industries
IFRS S1, because it lists industry-specific metrics for port operators
GRI, because it reports impacts on people and is the broadest standard for every stakeholder
questions.why: SASB is the standard built around industry-specific metrics selected for their likely effect on investor value, which is exactly what the investors asked for.

questions.prompt: A manufacturer collected a full year of energy and waste data without deciding which standard its report would follow. Later it decides the report must cover climate governance and climate risk management, as TCFD structures them. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: No change is needed, because TCFD only asks for financial data that the company already has
The ISSB will accept any layout, so the team can publish the existing data as it is
The report is compliant automatically, because ESG topics already cover TCFD structure
The governance and risk-management items are missing from the data, so the team must gather them again and the report is delayed
questions.why: Data gathered without the chosen standard in mind can lack required items, forcing re-collection and delay, which is the consequence the teaching text describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how GRI, SASB, TCFD and the IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards differ from one another, and how all of them differ from ESG disclosures in general. Name one limit or tradeoff of relying on a single framework.
lessons.modelAnswer: ESG is the umbrella: environmental, social and governance topics, and any statement a company makes about them is an ESG disclosure. The frameworks are the rulebooks. GRI is broad and impact-focused, covering a company's effects on the economy, environment and people for many audiences. SASB is industry-specific and focuses on financially material metrics for investors. TCFD is limited to climate and organizes content into governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets; the IFRS S1 and S2 standards carry this forward into a global baseline. The tradeoff of relying on one framework is that it may miss topics that matter to other stakeholders, so a team may need to combine frameworks or add disclosures beyond its chosen standard.
rubricPoints: ESG names broad topic areas, while a framework specifies what to report and how.
GRI reports impacts broadly for many stakeholders; SASB gives industry-specific, investor-focused metrics.
TCFD covers climate risk through four areas, and IFRS S1 and S2 carry its work forward.
A single framework can leave out topics that other stakeholders care about.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining how the frameworks differ from each other and from ESG, which no listed mission or planned engine practises directly.

lessons.plain: Sustainability in a project means doing the work so it causes less harm to the environment and to people, while still delivering what was promised. Regeneration goes a step further: the project aims to leave the local site or community better off than it found it, not just less damaged. Resilience is the ability of a project, or the thing it builds, to absorb a shock such as a flood, a heatwave or a supplier failure, and to recover quickly with its essential functions intact. Think of a bridge designed to lose less when a storm hits, or a community project that restores a wetland rather than merely avoiding drainage. Together these three ideas shape how you plan, buy and build.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project team is building a warehouse on a floodplain. Before reading anything, what two design choices would you expect them to make to reduce harm to the site and to keep the warehouse running after a flood?
lessons.teach: Sustainability, in a project setting, means delivering the work while cutting its negative impact: fewer emissions, less waste, less water drawn from local supplies, and less harm to people nearby. A negative impact is any measurable harm the project causes to the environment or community. Regeneration is the next step: the project actively restores something, such as soil, habitat or local skills, so the site ends up with more capacity than before. Resilience is the ability of a project, or the asset it creates, to withstand an extreme event such as flooding, heat or a supplier collapse, and to recover quickly with its essential functions intact. Why it works: most damage is cheaper to prevent in design than to repair afterwards, and a plan that names its hazards in advance can be tested before the hazard arrives. Worked example: a team builds a data centre on a coastal plot. Step 1: they pull historical flood records and set a design flood level. Step 2: they place critical electrical equipment above that level, so a flood does not stop the building. Step 3: they recycle cooling water rather than drawing fresh water from the local aquifer, which reduces negative impact. Step 4: they set a recovery time target and test a failover to a second site. Common mistake: treating resilience as just a backup copy of data while ignoring whether power and cooling can keep running. Consequence: if the substation floods and the equipment was not raised, the site is offline for weeks, and the emergency rebuild adds emissions and waste that the sustainability plan never counted. Resilience and sustainability are linked, because an asset that fails early wastes the materials that went into building it.

questions.prompt: A team builds a grain mill in a semi-arid district. Step 1: they set a ceiling on water draw based on the district's recorded rainfall, so the mill never takes more than the local aquifer can recharge. Step 2: they install a closed-loop wash system that recycles process water. Step 3: they fund replanting of a degraded riverbank with native reeds, so the site leaves behind more soil and habitat than it found. Step 4 is missing. The mill depends on one supplier for the fuel that dries grain during the wet season, and the team needs a resilience step that addresses that single point of failure. Which step completes the resilience part of the plan?
choices: Replace the wash system with a larger unit so that more water can be recycled.
Set a target to reduce the number of staff on site during the harvest.
Qualify a second fuel supplier and test a switchover to it before the wet season begins.
Measure the mill's emissions in tonnes of CO2 equivalent each quarter and publish the figures.
questions.why: Resilience means the asset can keep its essential functions and recover quickly from a disruption such as a supplier collapse, and qualifying and testing a second supplier does exactly that, while the other choices address emissions, water use or staffing rather than recovery.

questions.prompt: A council plants 40 hectares of native woodland on farmland that was stripped of topsoil years ago. Over time the woodland builds new soil, brings back insects and birds, and gives local workers forestry skills they did not have before. Which term best describes what the project is doing?
choices: Sustainability, because the project reduces the negative impact of the farmland's past use.
Resilience, because the woodland will withstand future droughts and floods.
Regeneration, because the site ends up with more capacity than it had before the project.
Negative impact, because planting trees disturbs the existing ground.
questions.why: Regeneration is the active restoration of soil, habitat or skills so the site has more capacity afterwards, which is what the woodland does, whereas sustainability only limits harm and resilience is about withstanding and recovering from extreme events.

questions.prompt: A solar farm is designed to withstand hailstorms. The team raises its inverters on a plinth above the expected hail-drift depth, which is a sound design step. However, the plan promises that any damaged inverter will be back in service within 48 hours, and the only spare inverters are stored 900 km away with a contractor who needs a week to ship them. What is the most important gap in the resilience plan?
choices: Raising the plinth is enough on its own, so no further recovery work is needed.
Hail damage to inverters is a sustainability question only, so resilience does not apply to them.
The 48-hour recovery target has no means behind it, because the spares cannot reach the site in that time, so the essential function cannot return that quickly.
Spare-part stock is a cost matter outside the project's scope, so it does not belong in the plan.
questions.why: Resilience requires that recovery is achievable, and a recovery target that cannot be met with the actual spares and logistics leaves the asset unable to restore its essential function in time.

questions.prompt: A textile firm says its new plant is sustainable because all of its fabric waste goes to a recycler. The plant still pumps heavily from a groundwater basin that is already falling in a dry region. Which reading of the project is correct?
choices: The plant is only sustainable if its water draw is also reduced, because recycling waste addresses one negative impact but leaves the groundwater harm untouched.
The plant is fully sustainable, because a project reduces its negative impact whenever any one measure is in place.
The plant is regenerative, because sending waste to a recycler adds capacity to the site.
The plant is resilient, because the recycler acts as a backup for the waste stream.
questions.why: Sustainability means reducing all measurable negative impacts the project causes, so a waste measure does not cancel out an unaddressed harm to the water supply.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between sustainability, regeneration and resilience in a project, and name one limit or tradeoff of designing for resilience.
lessons.modelAnswer: Sustainability means reducing the harm a project does, so less carbon, waste and water use, and less damage to nearby people and ecosystems. Regeneration asks for more than that: the project should leave the site with greater capacity than before, such as restored habitat or improved soil. Resilience is about shocks. It means the project or asset can take a hit, like a flood or a supplier failure, keep its essential functions running, and recover fast. A key tradeoff is cost. Raising equipment above a flood level or building a second site adds capital spend and material use, which can itself work against sustainability goals. So the team has to justify that extra material against the damage a failure would cause, and document the choice so the tradeoff is visible to the sponsor.
rubricPoints: Defines sustainability as reducing negative environmental and social impact
Distinguishes regeneration as restoring capacity beyond the original state
Defines resilience as withstanding and recovering from extreme events
Names a real tradeoff, such as extra cost or materials for resilience measures

suggested.rationale: Explaining the three terms and their tradeoff to a teammate is the core skill here, and no listed mission covers sustainability concepts.

lessons.plain: PRiSM stands for Projects Integrating Sustainable Methods. It is a way of running projects that treats environmental, social and economic effects as part of the job rather than an afterthought. Traditional project management asks whether a project delivers on time, on budget and to scope. PRiSM keeps those questions and adds whether the project's outcomes are good for people, the planet and the local economy over its whole life. Its life cycle is the sequence of stages a project moves through, and sustainability checks are built into each stage.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project team has a schedule, budget and scope that all look healthy, but nobody recorded what the project would do to local water use. Which stage of the work was most likely skipped, and what would you add to catch this earlier?
lessons.teach:
A project life cycle is the ordered set of phases a project passes through from start to finish. Each phase produces deliverables, meaning tangible outputs such as a plan, a register or a report, which the next phase depends on. PRiSM uses a life cycle of this kind but adds sustainability work to each phase. Traditional project management focuses mainly on scope, schedule, cost, quality and risk. PRiSM keeps all of these and adds the impacts of the project on people, the environment and the economy, along with how those impacts are tracked after the project closes.

Why it works: a sustainability problem is far cheaper to fix when it is still a decision on paper than when the asset is already built. So the method places a sustainability check at the stage where the relevant choice is made, and it records what was decided so later phases can carry it forward.

Worked example: a team proposing a new warehouse. In initiation, they record a sustainability goal for the project, such as limiting construction waste. In planning, they turn that goal into a measurable plan element with a target and a named owner. In execution, they report progress against that target. At closure, they hand over the measured results and the arrangements for monitoring them after handover. Each phase has a named output that the next phase picks up.

Common mistake: treating sustainability as a single report written at the end. The output of each phase is what makes the sustainability work traceable, and a closing report cannot recover decisions that were never recorded earlier.

Consequence: if the planning-phase target is missing, the execution team has nothing to measure, and the project can close on budget while its impact goes unmeasured. PRiSM therefore asks the project manager to read the life cycle as a chain of deliverables, not as a list of stages to pass through.

questions.prompt: A regional hospital is replacing its laundry washers with water-efficient models. Work through the chain as the team does it. In initiation, the team records a sustainability goal: reduce water used per kilogram of linen washed. In planning, they set a target of 4 litres per kilogram and name the facilities engineer as its owner. In execution, they report monthly meter readings against that target. The initiation step is the one left blank: before any design work starts, the team ______. Which completion fills the gap?
choices: sets the contractor's payment milestones for the washer installation
waits until planning to decide whether sustainability work applies at all
records a sustainability goal for the project in a form planning can pick up
writes one sustainability summary for the hospital board at handover
questions.why: Initiation's named output is the recorded sustainability goal, which planning then turns into a measurable target, so that goal must exist before planning begins.

questions.prompt: A road-resurfacing manager says PRiSM is traditional project management with a sustainability label added at the end. Which statement best corrects this?
choices: PRiSM is a separate method run alongside the project, so the project team does not need to change its plan.
PRiSM replaces scope, schedule, cost, quality and risk with impact measures, so those controls are no longer needed.
PRiSM keeps the traditional areas of scope, schedule, cost, quality and risk, adds the project's impacts on people, the environment and the economy, and tracks those impacts after closure.
PRiSM only adds a sustainability report written during closure, leaving every other phase unchanged.
questions.why: PRiSM retains the traditional management areas and adds people, environment and economy impacts with post-closure tracking, rather than replacing or bolting on a single report.

questions.prompt: A community solar installation closes on budget and on schedule, but no measurable sustainability target was recorded during planning. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The schedule slips, because the whole project must be re-planned to add a target.
Closure automatically creates a target from the final cost report, so measurement is recovered.
The project's impact cannot be measured, because execution has no target to report progress against.
The project is safe, because sustainability is checked only in the end-of-project report.
questions.why: Without a planning-phase target, execution has nothing to measure against, so the project can close successfully on cost and time while its impact goes unmeasured.

questions.prompt: A stadium lighting upgrade is now in the execution phase. Which output does this phase produce for the project's sustainability work?
choices: A final measured result of energy saved, handed to the operations team at closure.
A sustainability goal recorded for the first time at the project's start.
Progress reports measured against the planned target, which closure will later use.
A list of stakeholders who will monitor the lights after handover.
questions.why: In execution, the team reports progress against the target set in planning, and those reports feed the closure phase; the final measured results belong to closure, not execution.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how PRiSM differs from traditional project management, and name one limit or tradeoff of applying the full PRiSM life cycle to a small project.
lessons.modelAnswer: Traditional project management is judged on scope, schedule, cost, quality and risk. PRiSM keeps those measures but adds the project's effects on people, the environment and the local economy, and it tracks those effects through every phase of the life cycle rather than in one report at the end. Each phase is expected to produce named deliverables that the next phase builds on, so a sustainability decision made early is carried forward and can be checked later. The main tradeoff is overhead. On a small project, recording sustainability targets, owners and measurements at every phase can cost more effort than the project's impact justifies, so the team should scale the depth of each deliverable to the size and risk of the work.
rubricPoints: PRiSM keeps traditional measures such as scope, schedule, cost, quality and risk and adds impacts on people, environment and economy.
Sustainability work is built into each life cycle phase, not left to a final report.
Each phase produces deliverables that the next phase depends on, so decisions are traceable.
A real limit or tradeoff is named, such as added overhead on small projects, and the response explains how to scale the effort.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly a set of concepts and named deliverables from the framework, with no hands-on OpsForge mission or planned engine that teaches it better than reading and explaining back.

lessons.plain: A project's life cycle is the set of stages it passes through, from first idea to close. PRiSM is a way of running projects that builds sustainability into those stages rather than adding it at the end. This objective is about reading a situation, saying which stage the project is in, and naming what that stage should produce or support: the people needed on the team, the document or output that is due, how risks and chances to improve are handled, how money is planned and tracked, and how the timeline is built. Think of a builder who knows foundations come before walls and who can name what is due at each step, rather than saying only follow the process.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team is halfway through building a new depot, and the sponsor asks what they should be producing right now. Before reading anything, what questions would you ask to answer well, and what answer would change depending on the replies?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A phase is one stage of the project life cycle, a block of work with its own starting conditions and outputs. A deliverable is a tangible output a phase must produce, such as a plan, a report, or an approved design. A supporting process is ongoing work that runs alongside the phases, such as managing risks and opportunities or tracking cost. In PRiSM, sustainability is part of each phase, so the question is never only what is the next task, but what must be true and produced before the project can move on.

Why it works. Each phase answers a different question. Early phases establish purpose and expected sustainability impact. Planning turns that into staffing, schedule, budget, and risk responses. Execution produces the work. Monitoring and closure check that the work still meets its sustainability aims and hand it over. Once you know the phase, you can predict what should already exist and what is missing.

Worked example. A team is three weeks into planning a water treatment upgrade. Step one: identify the phase as planning. Step two: staffing: name the roles needed, including someone accountable for the sustainability measures. Step three: deliverables: the plan setting sustainability targets and the impact analysis must be approved before equipment is procured. Step four: risks and opportunities go into a register with named owners. Step five: cost and finance: a budget baseline that includes sustainability costs and expected savings. Step six: schedule: milestones tied to those approvals.

Common mistake. Treating the life cycle as a checklist to finish, and skipping the early impact analysis so sustainability is checked only at closure.

Consequence. If the plan is missing, procurement buys equipment that cannot meet the agreed targets, and the rework lands during execution, when it costs the most.

The phase tells you which deliverable and supporting process the project owes right now, and skipping it moves the cost of finding the gap to the most expensive point.

questions.prompt: A regional dairy co-operative is in the execution phase of installing a biogas digester. Step one: the phase is execution. Step two: staffing: a named person on site is accountable for the sustainability measures. Step three: deliverables: the installed unit is commissioned and checked against the sustainability targets approved during planning before handover. Step four: the risk and opportunity register is updated, and each new item has a named owner. Step five is missing. What finance item must the team have in place at this point?
choices: Remove sustainability costs from the budget so that spend reports match the purchase orders.
Delay all cost tracking until closure, when the final figures are known.
Update the cost baseline to record sustainability costs and expected savings, and track actual spend against it.
Reissue the original planning budget unchanged, since the sustainability costs were already approved.
questions.why: During execution the cost baseline must carry the sustainability costs and expected savings, and actual spend is tracked against it so gaps show up early.

questions.prompt: A community solar farm has finished installation and is entering the monitoring phase. Which supporting activity fits this phase best?
choices: Rewriting the staffing plan so the installation crew can be reassigned to a new site.
Starting a fresh impact analysis for a second farm before this one is checked.
Tracking actual electricity output against the sustainability impact expected in the approved impact analysis.
Closing the project budget so that no further sustainability costs can be recorded.
questions.why: Monitoring checks that delivered work still meets the sustainability aims set in the early phases, so output is compared against the approved expectations.

questions.prompt: A bakery retrofit team bought new ovens before its impact analysis was approved. Months later they found the energy target could not be met. Which earlier step was skipped?
choices: Approving the impact analysis and sustainability targets before procurement.
Naming a staff member to log daily oven temperatures.
Holding a closure review once the ovens were installed.
Creating a schedule with milestones after the ovens were delivered.
questions.why: The impact analysis and targets must be approved before equipment is bought, because procurement locks in what the project can achieve.

questions.prompt: A river restoration project is in its planning phase. Which schedule approach matches the PRiSM method?
choices: Leave out milestones until the project is closed, so the timeline stays flexible.
Schedule a single milestone at the end of the project for all approvals together.
Set the first milestone for the day the planting crew arrives on site.
Tie milestones to the approval of the sustainability targets and impact analysis, so that later work waits for them.
questions.why: In planning, the schedule's milestones should be linked to the approvals that the next work depends on, such as the targets and impact analysis.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would work out which PRiSM life-cycle deliverable or supporting process a project needs right now, and name one limit of relying on the phase alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by locating the project in its phase, by checking which decisions have already been approved. Then I would name the specific output that phase must produce before the next phase starts, for example an approved sustainability plan during planning, and check which supporting processes must be running: staffing needs, a risk and opportunity register, a cost baseline, and a schedule with milestones tied to approvals. The limit is that phases overlap in real projects. A team may be executing one workstream while still planning another, so I would check each workstream rather than assume the whole project sits in one phase. Also, the phase tells me what should exist, not whether its content is good enough, so I would still review each deliverable with the sponsor.
rubricPoints: Identifies the project's current phase from the approvals and work already done
Names a specific deliverable that the phase must produce before moving on
Connects supporting processes such as staffing, risk, cost, and scheduling to that phase
States a real limit, such as overlapping phases or the phase not confirming content quality

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style phase scenario and choosing the right deliverable adds the most to this objective, and no listed mission or engine matches it directly.

lessons.plain: PRiSM is a framework for running projects so they account for environmental, social and economic effects, not just scope, time and cost. Its life cycle has phases, but some work does not belong to any single phase and instead runs alongside all of them. These are the supporting processes. Think of them as habits that keep a project honest while it moves through its stages: talking with the people affected, estimating realistically, building the team, buying responsibly, and checking results against sustainability goals. Knowing which supporting process a situation calls for is the skill this objective tests.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project team must choose between two suppliers for a large batch of materials. The cheaper supplier is slightly faster but has no information about its environmental practices. Which PRiSM supporting process is most directly involved in this decision, and what would you ask the supplier for before signing?
lessons.teach:
A supporting process is a piece of PRiSM work that runs across the whole project rather than belonging to one life-cycle phase. The five you need to recognise are stakeholder engagement (identifying the people affected and gathering and sharing their input), estimation (predicting cost, effort and sustainability impacts, not only money and time), team development (building the skills and habits the team needs), sustainable procurement (choosing suppliers and buying goods using environmental and social criteria as well as price), and performance monitoring (measuring results against sustainability targets and a baseline). Each one is triggered by a question. Who is affected? What will this really cost in every sense? What skills are missing? Where is the money and material going? Did we achieve what we said?

Worked example: a school building retrofit is in its planning phase. The team asks residents and staff what they need, which is stakeholder engagement. They estimate energy savings and embodied carbon alongside construction cost, which is estimation. They ask bidders for evidence of material sourcing before scoring offers, which is sustainable procurement. After handover, they compare metered energy use with the baseline recorded before work began, which is performance monitoring.

A common mistake is treating these processes as a one-off task at kickoff and then forgetting them. Another is assigning them to nobody because they feel like background work. In a running project, an estimate that ignores sustainability impacts forces rework when a later phase must add them, often after money has already been committed.

Supporting processes keep sustainability decisions connected across every phase of the project.

questions.prompt: A regional hospital laundry is switching detergent supplier. Step one: the team scores tender bids partly on how much water each product uses per kilogram washed, not on price alone. Step two: before the new contract starts, the team records current water use per kilogram as a reference point. Step three is missing from this account: before writing the tender, the team asks the laundry staff and ward nurses what problems they have with the current detergent and what they need from a replacement. Step four: six weeks after the switch, the team compares meter readings with the reference point from step two. Which supporting process does the missing step belong to?
choices: Stakeholder engagement
Team development
Estimation
Performance monitoring
questions.why: Asking the people affected what they need and gathering their input is the definition of stakeholder engagement, which is the process the missing step describes.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches the supporting process called estimation in PRiSM?
choices: Predicting cost, effort and sustainability impacts together rather than money and time alone
Building the skills the team needs by running training sessions in the first month
Measuring results against sustainability targets after a project closes
Choosing suppliers using environmental and social criteria alongside price
questions.why: Estimation in this course means predicting every kind of cost and impact, including sustainability impacts, not just money and time.

questions.prompt: A municipal library refit is in its delivery phase. Library staff have not yet been trained to run the newly installed heat pumps, and the team needs to decide which supporting process covers closing that gap. Which process is it?
choices: Sustainable procurement
Team development
Stakeholder engagement
Performance monitoring
questions.why: Building the skills and habits the team needs, such as operating new equipment, is the purpose of team development.

questions.prompt: A school district sets energy and water targets at kickoff of a building project, then never compares later meter readings with the figures recorded before work began. Which supporting process has failed, and what is the consequence?
choices: Performance monitoring, so the team cannot tell whether the results match the targets or the baseline
Sustainable procurement, so the suppliers were not scored on energy use
Estimation, so the team cannot tell whether the cost forecast was right
Stakeholder engagement, so residents were not asked about the targets
questions.why: Performance monitoring is the process of measuring results against targets and a baseline, and skipping it means nobody learns whether the project achieved what it said.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what PRiSM supporting processes are, using one example from your own experience or from a project you know. Name one limit or tradeoff of relying on them, such as cost, time or the quality of the data available.
lessons.modelAnswer: Supporting processes are the PRiSM activities that run through the whole project, not inside one phase. In my example, a community water project, we ran stakeholder engagement continuously, because residents raised concerns about water quality late in the work when we had only consulted at the start. The tradeoff is that continuous engagement takes time and staff, and it can slow decisions. We also relied on estimates built from limited data, so the sustainability impact figures were uncertain. A good PM names that uncertainty openly and schedules the monitoring to check whether the estimates held. Without that, the team may trust numbers that were only ever rough guesses.
rubricPoints: Defines supporting processes as work that runs across all phases rather than within one
Gives a concrete example that uses at least one of the five named processes
Names a real limit or tradeoff such as time, cost, staffing or data quality
Explains how monitoring or re-checking reduces the risk of relying on uncertain estimates

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right supporting process for a described situation is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario, and no listed OpsForge mission covers project management.

lessons.plain: P5 is a way of looking at a project's effects across five areas at once: the thing being made, the way it is made, the people involved, the natural environment, and the economic value it creates. Each area breaks down into smaller groupings, and each grouping contains specific items you can point to. Learning this vocabulary matters because it lets you say exactly which kind of impact you mean, instead of vaguely calling a project 'sustainable'. Think of it like a map legend: you need to know what the symbols stand for before you can read the terrain.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project replaces a fleet of old diesel vans with electric vans. Before any teaching, name two different kinds of effect this change could have, and say which one you would be most likely to overlook when writing the project plan.
lessons.teach:
A P5 category is one of the five big groups the standard uses to sort impacts: Product (the deliverable itself), Process (how the work is done), People (the humans affected), Planet (the natural environment), and Prosperity (economic value and resilience). A subcategory is a narrower slice inside one category, such as lifespan or servicing under Product. An element is a specific item you can point to and assess, such as the battery pack of a vehicle. A lens is a question you ask of a subcategory to bring out impacts, such as how long something will last and what happens at end of life. A perspective is the viewpoint from which you judge an impact, such as whose view you take and over what time span. Together these give a team shared language.

The reason this works is that a vague word hides what is actually changing. Naming the category, subcategory and element forces precision, so two people analysing the same project reach findings they can compare.

Worked example: a city replaces forty diesel vans with electric vans. Step one, Product: the subcategory is lifespan and the element is the battery pack; the lens asks how many years the battery lasts. Step two, Process: the subcategory is efficiency and the element is the overnight charging schedule. Step three, People: the element is driver training on the new vehicles. Step four, perspective: the city's view over ten years differs from the depot staff's view this year, so the same battery item can carry different weight depending on viewpoint.

Common mistake: treating the five categories as separate silos and filing an impact in only one place. The battery's disposal effect on Planet then goes unexamined.

In a running programme, a missed Planet element usually surfaces years later as a disposal cost nobody budgeted for. The vocabulary is what turns a vague concern into an item that can be assessed.

questions.prompt: A regional water utility is replacing aging pumping stations with variable-speed pumps. Work through the P5 trace. Step 1, Product: the subcategory is lifespan and the element is the pump impeller; the lens asks how many years it runs before it needs replacing. Step 2, Process: the subcategory is servicing and the element is the quarterly maintenance visit; the lens asks how often the visits are needed. Step 3 is missing. Step 4, perspective: the utility's view over twenty years differs from the pump station operator's view this year. Which entry correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Planet: the element is the station's electricity meter, and the subcategory is energy use across the year.
People: the element is the maintenance crew's training on the new speed controllers, and the lens asks how confidently operators can diagnose a fault.
Prosperity: the element is the utility's credit rating, and the lens asks how the rating changes after the purchase.
Product: the element is the old pump casing, and the subcategory is lifespan, so the casing's life is recorded again.
questions.why: Step 3 is the People category, since the crew's training is a human-facing element, and the lens asks about the crew's capability, which is the step that completes the trace.

questions.prompt: In the P5 vocabulary, which term names the viewpoint from which you judge an impact, such as whose view you take and over what time span?
choices: Perspective
Subcategory
Lens
Element
questions.why: A perspective is defined as the viewpoint from which an impact is judged, while a lens is a question asked of a subcategory, an element is a specific item, and a subcategory is a narrower slice within a category.

questions.prompt: A hospital laundry project plans to replace its old industrial washers. The team's risk log says only 'sustainability: water.' Why is this entry weak for a P5 analysis?
choices: It names neither the category, the subcategory, nor the element, so two analysts cannot compare their findings.
It is too specific, because a P5 entry should always cover all five categories in one line.
It uses a lens where a perspective should be, which only matters for portfolio-level reporting.
Water is not one of the five P5 categories, so it cannot be recorded at all.
questions.why: The teaching text stresses that a vague word hides what is changing, and naming the category, subcategory and element is what lets two people reach comparable findings.

questions.prompt: A council and the plant operator both assess the same variable-speed pump. The council looks at twenty years of costs; the operator looks at this year's workload. Which statement about their assessments is correct?
choices: Both must reach the same weight, because the element and category are identical for both.
The council's view should be ignored, because perspectives only apply to Planet impacts.
The operator's view is always the correct one, since the team on site knows the equipment best.
The same pump element can carry different weight, because the viewpoint and time span shape how the impact is judged.
questions.why: The teaching text explains that the same element can carry different weight depending on the perspective taken, such as whose view is used and over what time span.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has heard the words P5 and lens but is still confused how categories, subcategories, elements, lenses and perspectives fit together. Then name one limit or tradeoff of using this vocabulary on a real project.
lessons.modelAnswer: Think of the five P5 categories as the big drawers in a filing cabinet: Product, Process, People, Planet and Prosperity. Inside each drawer are subcategories, which are the folders, such as lifespan or fairness. Each folder holds elements, the individual documents, such as a specific battery or a specific training programme. A lens is the question you ask of a folder to pull out what matters, and a perspective is whose view you take and over what time span. The limit is that the categories are a sorting aid, not a verdict: a single item often belongs in several drawers, and if the team forces each item into just one, real effects go missing. So the vocabulary helps us be precise, but we still have to check across categories.
rubricPoints: Defines the five P5 categories in plain terms
Explains that subcategories narrow a category and elements are specific assessable items
Distinguishes a lens (question asked) from a perspective (viewpoint and timeframe)
Names a limit such as items spanning several categories or the risk of forcing a single placement

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly shared vocabulary and definitions, which is best learned by reading the terms and their relationships before any hands-on work.

lessons.plain: When a project changes something people will use or something people do, it leaves effects beyond the budget and the schedule. P5 impact analysis is a way of examining those effects through five lenses: Product, Process, People, Planet and Prosperity. This objective covers two of the five areas. Product lenses ask how long the thing you deliver will stay useful and how easily it can be kept running. Process lenses ask whether the way work gets done wastes less, actually achieves its purpose, and treats the people involved fairly. Asking these questions before work starts helps you spot costs that a normal plan would miss.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team is replacing a paper timesheet with a new app. Before reading anything, name two things about the app that could make it a worse deal for the company over five years, even if it launches on time and on budget.
lessons.teach:
A P5 lens is a specific question you ask about a project to reveal impacts that a standard cost-and-schedule view hides. The Product lenses look at the thing being delivered. Lifespan is how long the product stays useful before it must be replaced. Servicing is the maintenance, repair, and updating needed to keep the product working, including how easy and costly that work is. The Process lenses look at how work is done. Efficiency is useful output compared with the time, money, materials, or energy consumed. Effectiveness is whether the process actually achieves the goal it exists for. Fairness is whether the burdens and benefits of the process are shared reasonably among the people it touches.

Why this works: a plan that only checks purchase price and delivery date treats ongoing costs as someone else's problem. Lifespan and servicing questions bring those costs into the open before they are locked in.

Worked example: a council plans to replace 500 streetlights. Step 1, lifespan: the new fixtures are rated for about 12 years, the old lamps for about 4, so fewer replacements are needed over time. Step 2, servicing: each fixture needs a crew with a lift truck, about 20 minutes per fixture, so the design should ask whether crews can reach fixtures without closing roads. Step 3, Process lens: efficiency asks how many crew-hours the replacement schedule consumes, effectiveness asks whether the lights actually reduce the problems they were bought to address, and fairness asks whether night callouts fall on the same few people every week.

Common mistake: treating lifespan as a datasheet number without considering the real operating conditions, or counting only the purchase price. In a running system, poor servicing access means every repair becomes a long outage, which the business pays for later.

questions.prompt: A regional water utility plans to replace 40 pressure-reducing valves housed in underground chambers. Step 1, lifespan: the new valves are rated for 15 years and the old ones for 6, but the chambers flood each spring, so the utility's own field records suggest the new valves will last about 10 years in practice, and the design should use that figure rather than the datasheet. Step 2, servicing: each valve needs a two-person confined-space entry taking about 90 minutes, so the design should ask whether these entries can be scheduled without cutting supply to nearby homes. Step 3, Process lens: [missing]. Which completion correctly applies the efficiency lens to this step?
choices: Efficiency: compare useful output, such as valves kept in service, with the crew-hours and entry permits consumed, and check whether another maintenance schedule gives more output per hour.
Efficiency: ask whether the project finished under budget, because a cheaper delivery is always the efficient outcome.
Efficiency: confirm the valve's pressure rating matches the mains, since a correctly rated valve is by definition an efficient one.
Efficiency: ask whether households near the chambers bear the outage burden more often than others, since that is what efficiency measures.
questions.why: Efficiency compares useful output with the time, money, materials, or energy consumed, so the correct completion measures valves kept in service against crew-hours and permits and looks for a better ratio.

questions.prompt: A hospital laundry service buys new washer-dryers whose manufacturer rates them for 14 years of life. Under the product lifespan lens, what should the team do with that figure?
choices: Estimate the useful life from the expected operating conditions, such as load, water quality, and hours of use, rather than relying only on the rating.
Replace the machines every 14 years regardless of their condition, because the rating sets a fixed schedule.
Ignore lifespan entirely and judge the purchase only by the price paid at delivery.
Accept the rating as the working life, since the manufacturer tested the machines.
questions.why: The lifespan lens asks how long a product stays useful under real conditions, so the team should adjust the rating to the actual operating environment instead of taking it at face value.

questions.prompt: A school district redraws its bus routes to reduce fuel use. Under the new plan, two rural villages carry the longest rides every single day, while other schools share their burden. Which P5 Process lens does this finding most directly raise?
choices: Efficiency, because the total fuel burned has fallen.
Fairness, because the burden of long rides is falling repeatedly on the same communities.
Effectiveness, because the buses still reach every school on time.
Lifespan, because the buses will wear out faster on long routes.
questions.why: Fairness asks whether the burdens and benefits of a process are shared reasonably among the people it touches, and a fixed group carrying the longest rides every day is a fairness issue.

questions.prompt: A cold-storage company selects compressors that are cheap to buy but require the whole unit to be removed from the plant for a bearing change. Which outcome best describes the consequence of ignoring servicing access in this choice?
choices: The compressors fail to meet their effectiveness goal because the unit size is wrong for the building.
Each routine repair becomes a long outage, and the real cost appears later as downtime rather than in the purchase price.
The compressor's purchase price rises after delivery because the supplier charges for access to the bearings.
The compressors become more efficient over time because fewer technicians are needed to maintain them.
questions.why: Poor servicing access turns every repair into a long outage, and the business pays for that later, which is exactly the hidden ongoing cost the servicing lens is meant to expose.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would apply the Product lenses of lifespan and servicing, and the Process lenses of efficiency, effectiveness and fairness, to a proposed project. Name one limit or tradeoff of doing this analysis.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would take the proposed project and ask four questions. For lifespan, how long will the delivered thing realistically stay useful under our actual conditions, not just the vendor's rating? For servicing, who will maintain it, how often, and how hard is it to reach and repair? For the process side, I would ask whether the work uses time and materials efficiently, whether it actually meets its goal, and whether the load and benefit fall fairly across the people involved. The main limit is that these answers are estimates made early, so they can be wrong, and the analysis takes time that a tight schedule may not allow. I would say that openly and revisit the answers as real data arrives, rather than presenting the early numbers as settled.
rubricPoints: Defines lifespan as the realistic useful life of the delivered product under actual conditions
Explains servicing as maintenance effort, access, and cost over the product's life
Distinguishes efficiency, effectiveness, and fairness as separate process questions
Names a real limit, such as early estimates being uncertain or time pressure

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style project scenario with lifespan, servicing, and process lenses adds the most, and no listed OpsForge mission or planned engine covers this content directly.

lessons.plain: After a project's sustainability impacts have been identified and scored, someone has to sort each finding into the right bucket and then tell the sponsor what the results mean. This objective is about that second half: taking each impact and filing it under the correct element of the P5 lens, which covers Product, Process, People, Planet and Prosperity, and then writing a closure status that is honest about what was found, what was done, and what was left open. Think of it like filing receipts into the right ledger columns, then writing the year-end summary from those columns.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project to replace a city bus depot's lighting cut electricity use, but it also moved 40 workers onto night shifts to finish the installation. Without any training, where would you file the night-shift effect, and why might one finding belong in more than one place?
lessons.teach:
A P5 impact analysis produces a list of impacts, each one a specific effect the project has on a product, a process, people, the planet, or prosperity (the economic and social wellbeing of the communities around it). Assigning an item to an element means choosing the most fitting named area within the P5 structure for that impact. An element sits under one of the five categories. Assignment is not a label applied once and forgotten: when an effect spreads into a second area, the analysis should record a secondary element as well as the primary one.
