Closure status reporting is the final summary written when the project ends. For each element it states what was found, what was acted on, and what remains open or was accepted as a residual risk.

Why this works: the five categories force a view of the whole project, so a reader can see at a glance whether effort went into only one area.

Worked example. A depot retrofit replaces old lights with efficient LEDs. Step 1: the energy saving is an effect on the planet, so it is filed under Planet. Step 2: moving 40 workers onto night shifts affects working hours and fatigue, so it is filed under People, with Process as a secondary element because the schedule changed how the work is done. Step 3: at closure, the report lists the energy saving as achieved, and the night-shift finding with the action taken (rest days added) and the item still open (fatigue survey not yet run).

Common mistake: writing a closure report that lists only the positive impacts, or filing the night-shift effect under Planet because it sits next to the energy result in the spreadsheet.

Consequence: the closure report usually feeds a portfolio dashboard. If the labor finding is buried, the next depot project repeats the same schedule and nobody sees the risk coming.

questions.prompt: A bakery replaces its gas ovens with one electric oven shared by three tenant businesses. Step 1: the drop in gas use is an effect on the planet, so it is filed under Planet. Step 2: the new booking rota changes when each tenant can trade, so the tenant income effect is filed under Prosperity as the primary element. The rota also changes the order in which the bakers make bread, so this impact spreads into a second area, and the analyst must record that second area. Step 3: at closure, the report records the gas saving as achieved and the tenant income finding with its action and open item. Which element should be recorded as the secondary element for the tenant income impact?
choices: People, because the bakers are the only staff affected
Product, because the loaves now have a different crust
Process, because the rota changes the order in which the bakers make bread
Planet, because the oven still saves energy
questions.why: The rota changes how the baking work is sequenced, which is a process effect, so Process is the fitting secondary element, while the crust change is a separate effect that would be filed on its own.

questions.prompt: A parcel courier's route software cuts engine idling and so reduces the fuel burned per delivery. Which element is the most fitting primary element for this impact?
choices: Prosperity
Planet
People
Product
questions.why: Reduced fuel burned is an effect on the environment, which the P5 structure files under Planet, and it is not primarily about wellbeing, staff, or the goods themselves.

questions.prompt: A hospital laundry closes its water-saving project. Its closure report lists only the water saving as achieved and says nothing about a staff heat-exposure finding that was partly handled. What is the main flaw in this report?
choices: It is acceptable, because closure reports should summarise achievements only
It omits what remains open or was accepted as residual risk, so a reader cannot see the unfinished findings
It is incomplete only if the number of elements reported is fewer than five
It should have filed the water saving under Prosperity instead of Planet
questions.why: A closure status report must state for each element what was found, what was acted on, and what remains open or was accepted as residual risk, so leaving out the partly handled heat-exposure finding hides the unfinished work.

questions.prompt: A school district's new bus timetable reduces diesel use, but it also means drivers start earlier and the seat-belt checks are now done at the depot instead of on the road. An analyst has recorded the diesel reduction as the primary Planet impact. How should the analysis treat the change that spreads into a second area?
choices: File the diesel reduction under Process so that it appears with the schedule change
Keep the primary Planet element and record a secondary element for the area the effect spreads into
Move the whole impact into People and delete the Planet entry
Record only the Planet element, since one impact can carry only one element
questions.why: When an effect spreads into a second area, the analysis should keep the primary element and also record a secondary element, so the spread is visible rather than hidden.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide which P5 element an impact belongs under, and name one limit of that decision when an impact affects several elements at once.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking where the effect actually lands: a person's working conditions, a product's life, a process step, the environment, or the economic wellbeing of a community. That picks the primary element. Then I would ask whether the same effect reaches another element and record that as secondary, so it does not get hidden. The limit is that element choice is a judgement, and two careful analysts can file the same item differently. So the record should show the reasoning, and the closure report should be checked against every element, not only the one where I placed an item. If I look only at the primary element, a serious labor effect can look like an environmental one and get less attention than it deserves.
rubricPoints: Assigns each impact to the element where its main effect lands, using the P5 categories.
Records secondary elements when one effect reaches more than one area.
Explains that assignment is a judgement and should show its reasoning.
Closure status covers every element, stating findings, actions taken and open items.
Does not present only the positive impacts as the final result.

suggested.rationale: Filing impacts and writing a closure status is best practised by reasoning through a messy project scenario, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this.

lessons.plain: People impacts are the effects a project has on the humans around it: the workers who build or run it, the neighbors and customers who live with it, and the wider society whose rights and trust it touches. Evaluating them means asking who is affected, whether work is safe and fair, whether anyone's basic rights are at risk, and whether the project's claims and dealings are honest. For example, a project that relies on a subcontractor paying below local wages, or that advertises a 'green' product that is not really greener, has People impacts even if its carbon numbers look good. The goal is to spot these risks early, while they are still cheap to fix, rather than discover them in a news story.
lessons.guessPrompt: A subcontractor on your project pays its workers well below local rates, but its work is on time and within budget. Should that matter to you as the project manager, and why?
lessons.teach: Start with the definitions. Decent work means paid work that is productive, safe, fairly rewarded, and respectful of workers' rights, including reasonable working hours and a way for workers to raise concerns. Labor practices are the way a project hires, pays, supervises and protects the people doing its work, including contractors and the subcontractors they bring in. Human rights considerations are the basic rights of people affected by the project, such as freedom from forced labor, safe access to water and land, and the right to be heard about changes to their community. Anti-corruption means no bribes, kickbacks or improper favors to win or keep work. Greenwashing means making environmental or social claims that are misleading or unsupported, so the project looks more responsible than it is. Why it works: People impacts are judged by who bears the cost and whether the process was fair. The biggest risks rarely sit with the project team's own staff; they sit in the supply chain, the host community, and the buyer's trust. Tracing the chain of people who touch the work is how the risk becomes visible. Worked example: a rail upgrade project. Step 1: list the groups affected, which are the main contractor's crew, agency staff supplying night workers, residents near the line, and passengers. Step 2: for the agency staff, check pay against local norms and whether recruitment fees are charged to workers. Step 3: for residents, check whether noise and access concerns were consulted on. Step 4: check the 'zero-emission' claim in the marketing, and whether the supplier's contract includes gifts to officials. Each finding gets an owner and a fix before the next stage gate. Common mistake: treating People impacts as a box ticked by one policy statement. A signed code of conduct does not prove that subcontractors pay fair wages. Consequence: if agency workers are underpaid and the fact surfaces mid-project, work may stop, the contract may be suspended, and the reputational damage can outlast the build. Evaluating People impacts means tracing the chain of people behind the work and testing claims against evidence, not reading a policy.

questions.prompt: A city council is extending a hospital wing. The builder employs its own crew directly, but night cleaners come from a labour broker, meaning an agency that supplies workers to a project and handles their hiring. The affected groups are the builder's crew, the broker's cleaners, residents of the apartment block next to the site, and the hospital's patients. Step 1 lists these groups. Step 2 checks that the cleaners' shift lengths stay within the limit written in the broker's contract and that cleaners can raise a complaint without losing their jobs. Step 3 is missing from this trace. Step 4 checks the council's public line that the wing is 'fully sustainable' against the energy certificate on file. Which step 3 completes the trace?
choices: Confirm that the builder's own crew belongs to a union, and skip the broker's records because the broker is not the builder's staff.
Ask the council to publish the broker's contract value so the public can compare it with other bids.
Ask patients to sign a code of conduct for the building site, since a signed code is the main evidence for People impacts.

Check whether the apartment residents were consulted about night-time noise and access changes, and record any gap with an owner and a fix before the next stage gate, meaning the checkpoint before the next phase.
questions.why: The residents are a named affected group whose right to be heard about changes to their community must be tested, and the missing step is the one that covers them.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines decent work as the course uses the term?
choices: Paid work that is productive but may be unsafe, as long as workers receive an occasional bonus.
Paid work that is productive, safe, fairly rewarded, respects workers' rights, keeps reasonable hours, and gives workers a way to raise concerns.
Any paid work at all, provided the employer has a signed code of conduct and sets the wage alone without any outside review.
Work paid at the legal minimum and done only by the project's own staff, with no concern for how hours are set.
questions.why: The teaching text defines decent work by these combined features, and the other options each drop at least one of them.

questions.prompt: A port-expansion contractor has a signed code of conduct covering all its staff. It says its subcontractors pay fair wages, but nobody has checked the subcontractors' pay records. What is the best reading under this course's approach?
choices: The signed code of conduct is enough evidence, so no further checking is needed for subcontractors.
Subcontractor pay is fair because the main contractor states it in its marketing material.
Unproven: a policy alone does not show fair subcontractor pay, so trace the chain of workers and test the claim against records.
Subcontractors fall outside the project's People review, so their pay does not need checking at all.
questions.why: The teaching text says a signed policy does not prove subcontractors pay fair wages, and that People claims must be traced and tested against evidence.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm pays a regional licensing officer a 'consultancy fee' to speed up permits for its new terminal. Which concept does this payment most directly breach?
choices: Decent work, meaning fair pay, safety and reasonable hours for the people doing the work.
Human rights considerations, meaning the basic rights of people affected by the project, such as access to water and land.
Anti-corruption, meaning no bribes, kickbacks or improper favors to win or keep work.
Greenwashing, meaning a misleading environmental claim made in marketing to look more responsible than the project is.
questions.why: A fee paid to an official to speed a permit is an improper favor given to win or keep work, which is what anti-corruption rules forbid.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would evaluate the People impacts of a project, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by mapping everyone the project touches: direct staff, contractors and their subcontractors, host communities, customers, and anyone whose rights could be affected. For each group I check labor practices (pay against local norms, hours, safety, whether workers pay recruitment fees), human rights risks (land, water, forced or child labor in the supply chain), and ethics (gifts or payments to officials, and whether public sustainability claims are backed by evidence). I record each finding with an owner and a fix before the next gate. The limit is that I can only verify what I can see. Deep supply chains and sensitive topics like corruption rely on audits, worker interviews and tips, which take time and may be incomplete. So my assessment is a reasoned, evidence-based view that needs refreshing as the project changes, not a guarantee that nothing is wrong.
rubricPoints: Identifies the affected groups, including contractors, subcontractors and communities, not only the project team
Checks labor practices such as pay, hours, safety and recruitment fees against a stated standard
Tests human rights risks and ethical claims, including anti-corruption and greenwashing, against evidence
States a limit or tradeoff, such as incomplete visibility into supply chains or reliance on audits

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a realistic exam-style scenario with conflicting People signals adds the most to this objective, and no listed mission covers it directly.

lessons.plain: When a project changes something in the world, it leaves marks beyond its own budget. Planet asks about the physical side: how much energy, material and travel the project uses, and what it leaves behind. Prosperity asks whether the project is worth doing for the wider economy and community, and whether it can adapt when conditions change. This objective is about spotting those effects in a scenario and judging them, not reciting a checklist of 'be green' ideas. Think of a road trip: the fuel cost matters, but so do the detours it forces on other drivers and whether the trip still makes sense if the route closes.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company plans a new warehouse built closer to its customers, so its delivery trucks drive fewer kilometres each day. Before any teaching, name one Planet effect of this decision and one Prosperity effect, and say which one you think a sponsor would weigh more heavily.
lessons.teach:
Planet impacts are effects on the physical environment. Under this lens, two things are worth tracing: transport, meaning how far materials, people and products move and by what means, and consumption, meaning how much energy, water and raw material the project and its output use over time. Prosperity impacts are effects on economic wellbeing. Within it, feasibility asks whether the project makes sense on paper and in practice, usually tested through a business case, which is a document setting out costs, benefits, risks and alternatives. Social return on investment, or social ROI, extends that idea by putting a value on benefits that do not show up as revenue, such as time saved for residents. Business agility is the ability to change direction at modest cost when conditions shift. Market and economic stimulation describes how spending, contracts and jobs flow into the local economy.

Worked example: a council plans to replace a bridge that forces a 40-minute detour. Step one: the materials come from a quarry 300 km away, so transport emissions are high, and the team compares a closer supplier. Step two: the business case sets construction cost against detour savings, and social ROI adds a value for the residents' recovered time. Step three: the work is split into phases so funding can pause without leaving a half-built structure, which is agility. Step four: contracts favour local firms, so spending stays in the area.

The common mistake is counting only the upfront cost. Recurring transport and consumption can outweigh a cheap build over its life, and stimulation is not automatically a benefit if it simply moves demand away from existing local businesses.

A P5 analysis should therefore name the Planet and Prosperity effects with a direction or rough size, not a general comment that the project is sustainable.

questions.prompt: A water utility plans to replace an aging pumping station that serves a town of 30,000 people. Step one: the new pumps would be built 500 km away and travel by road, so the team also prices a maker 90 km away and estimates the emissions gap between the two routes. Step two: the business case sets the capital cost against a 25-year energy saving, since the new pumps draw 120 kW against the old 180 kW, and it adds a value for fewer emergency callouts. Step three: the installation is split into two stages so the second can wait if demand falls. Step four is missing: the installation contract is worth 2 million and the team must decide how to check its market and economic effect on the town. Which completion of step four is correct?
choices: Note that stimulation is always a benefit, so no check is needed before the contract is awarded.
Accept the lowest bid, since the upfront cost is the only figure that changes the contract's economic effect on the town.
Drop the contract from the analysis, since the team has already counted the upfront cost in the business case.
Check where the contract's spending lands and record any lost local spending as a prosperity effect with a rough size.
questions.why: Market and economic stimulation tracks how spending and jobs flow into the local economy, so a distant award that moves money away from local businesses should be recorded with a direction and rough size.

questions.prompt: A tram operator's team must change route plans when rider numbers shift, and it wants to do so without large losses. Which best describes the idea of business agility in this situation?
choices: Spending the full budget early so that no funds are left unused.
Measuring the number of local jobs created by each route change.
The ability to change direction at modest cost when conditions shift.
Keeping the original route plan fixed so that contracts stay stable.
questions.why: Business agility is defined as the ability to change direction at modest cost when conditions shift, which is what the tram team is trying to do.

questions.prompt: A school district buys desks from a maker 700 km away. A maker 60 km away charges 8% more. Under the Planet lens, what is the right first analysis?
choices: Assume the nearer maker is always greener and skip any comparison of price or route.
Trace the distance and transport mode for each supplier and estimate the emissions gap between them.
Choose the cheaper desk, because transport only matters as a prosperity question.
Ignore distance, since desks are a one-off purchase and their transport does not recur.
questions.why: The transport part of the Planet lens asks how far products move and by what means, so the correct first step is to trace each route and give the emissions difference a direction and rough size.

questions.prompt: A library replaces its building's heating with a cheap gas unit that needs frequent heavy fuel deliveries. The business case compares only the purchase prices of the options. What is the main flaw?
choices: The flaw is that the unit should have been bought from a closer manufacturer only, with no cost comparison at all.
The business case ignores recurring transport and consumption, which can outweigh a cheap build over the unit's life.
The gas unit has no social return on investment, so the whole project is not worth considering.
The library's book budget should have been included in the heating business case as a cost.
questions.why: The common mistake is counting only the upfront cost, and recurring transport and consumption over the system's life can outweigh a cheap purchase price.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what the Planet and Prosperity lenses ask a project team to check, using one example of each, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on a business case alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: Planet asks about the physical footprint of a project: how far things travel, how much energy, water and material get used, and what waste results. Prosperity asks whether the project is worth it for the wider economy and community, and whether it can adapt. For Planet, a new supplier that cuts a 500 km haul to 50 km reduces transport emissions and probably lowers cost too. For Prosperity, the business case might show a payback of seven years, and social ROI might add the value of residents' saved travel time. The limit is that a business case usually values what can be priced. It can understate environmental costs and community benefits that have no market price, and it often assumes a fixed plan. So I would present the business case alongside the transport and consumption figures, with a note on how the plan could be scaled back if funding shifts.
rubricPoints: Names transport and consumption as Planet effects and gives a direction or rough size for each.
Explains that feasibility is tested with a business case and, where relevant, social ROI.
Connects business agility to the ability to change course at modest cost.
Distinguishes genuine market stimulation from demand simply shifted between local firms.
States a limit of relying on priced benefits alone.

suggested.rationale: Judging Planet and Prosperity effects across competing options in a scenario is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style situation, and no listed mission covers this.

lessons.plain: When a company or project reports on its environmental, social and governance performance, it cannot list everything it does. Materiality is the test for what goes in. Information is material when leaving it out, or getting it wrong, could change what a reasonable reader decides, such as an investor choosing where to put money or a community deciding whether to trust a project. Think of a packing list for a trip: you note the passport, not every sock you own. The same filter keeps a sustainability report focused and honest, so the important impacts are visible and the trivial ones do not bury them.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project's sustainability report could list 200 small facts, including the office's paper-cup count and a spill that harmed a nearby stream. Which should the report make sure readers see first, and why?
lessons.teach:
Materiality is the principle that a piece of information belongs in a report when it could reasonably influence the decisions of the people who read it. ESG stands for environmental, social and governance performance. A disclosure is any statement a project or organisation publishes about that performance. A stakeholder is anyone who is affected by the project or who relies on its report, such as investors, lenders, regulators, workers and nearby residents.

There are two common lenses. Financial materiality asks whether a topic could affect cost, revenue, fines, delays or value. Impact materiality asks whether the project itself causes significant effects on people or the planet, whatever the money impact. Many frameworks look at both, which is sometimes called double materiality.

Worked example: a road-building project has four candidate topics. Office paper use is small in scale and has little effect on any decision, so it is not material. Night-time noise affects a few residents and may bring complaints, so it is worth a short note. Runoff from the works into a stream is severe, is regulated, and could cause fines or a stop-work order, so it is material. A serious labour finding at a major subcontractor could change lender and worker decisions, so it is material. Each judgment rests on scale, severity, likelihood and effect on decisions.

Common mistake: keeping only flattering facts. Dropping bad news because it looks poor is a form of greenwashing, and it misleads the people relying on the report.

In a running project, omitting a material risk means investors or lenders may commit money on a false picture. When the problem surfaces later, the report must be corrected, which damages trust and can carry legal exposure. Materiality is therefore a judgment the project manager must document, not a checklist to skip.

questions.prompt: A water utility is replacing 12 km of town water mains. The team sorts four candidate topics for its ESG disclosure. Topic A is paper invoices printed in the site office. The scale is small and no decision would change, so it is not material. Topic B is excavation dust reaching a primary school 150 m away, with 30 parent complaints logged in one week. The effect on children is severe, and the regulator is likely to take interest, so it is material under the impact lens. Topic C is a planned two-day shutdown of water supply to 4,000 homes. It could trigger regulatory penalties and change customer and lender decisions, so it is material. Topic D is a contractor paying six local suppliers 25 days late. The amounts are small, the risk of a supply stoppage is low, and no reader would change a decision because of it. Step missing: the team has not yet recorded the verdict for Topic D and the reason for it. Which entry completes the assessment?
choices: Material, because any late payment is a legal breach that must be disclosed.
Not material, because scale, severity, likelihood and effect on decisions are all low, so no reader would reasonably change a decision.
Material, because local supplier goodwill is a financial asset that the report must value.
Not material, because late payments are financial matters and ESG reports exclude finance entirely.
questions.why: Materiality is judged by whether the information could reasonably influence readers' decisions, weighing scale, severity, likelihood and effect on decisions, and Topic D is low on every one of these.

questions.prompt: A solar farm developer is preparing a sustainability report for its lenders. Which statement best describes materiality as it applies to what goes into that report?
choices: Information goes in when it could reasonably influence the decisions of people who read the report.
Information goes in only when a law requires it, so the developer avoids judgment calls.
Only figures that show the project in a favourable light are included, to keep the report short.
Every measured value goes in, so that readers can judge the project for themselves.
questions.why: Materiality is the principle that information belongs in a report when it could reasonably influence readers' decisions, which is a judgment rather than a rule of including everything or only what the law names.

questions.prompt: A port operator expands a container terminal. Its internal monitoring shows an ammonia spike in a nearby coastal lagoon, and the environment agency has issued a formal warning about it. The operator's draft ESG report leaves the spike out because the rest of the year looks good. What is the main problem with this draft?
choices: The report is too long, so the spike should be moved to an appendix.
Leaving out a regulator-flagged problem because it looks poor is greenwashing, and it misleads the people relying on the report.
The report should wait until the agency closes the warning before any disclosure.
The spike is a financial matter, so it belongs only in the accounts.
questions.why: Dropping bad news because it looks poor is a form of greenwashing that misleads readers, and a regulator-flagged effect could influence readers' decisions, so it is likely material.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs a delivery depot where lorries idle overnight. Residents have complained that the engine noise and exhaust disrupt their sleep, but the company's own costs and fines are unaffected. Which lens should the project manager use first to judge whether this topic is material, and why?
choices: The impact lens, because the project itself causes a significant effect on nearby people whatever the money impact.
The financial lens only, because impact effects can be assessed only once they cost money.
The financial lens, because the company's costs and fines are unaffected, so the topic cannot be material.
Neither lens, because overnight activity is outside the scope of an ESG report.
questions.why: Impact materiality asks whether the project itself causes significant effects on people or the planet regardless of money impact, so the residents' disrupted sleep is the relevant test even though costs are unchanged.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is drafting the project's sustainability report what materiality means here, how you would decide whether a topic belongs in the report, and one limit or tradeoff of that judgment.
lessons.modelAnswer: Materiality means a topic goes in the report if leaving it out or misstating it could change what a reasonable reader decides. For each candidate topic I ask two questions. Could it affect money, such as fines, delays, cost or value? Does the project itself significantly affect people or the planet? I weigh scale, severity and likelihood, then check whether the answer would change a lender's or a community's decision. The main limit is that the judgment is subjective, so two people can disagree. The tradeoff is between a short, readable report and a complete one. To stay honest, I write down why each topic was included or left out, and I keep unflattering material information in, even when it is uncomfortable.
rubricPoints: Defines materiality as information that could reasonably influence readers' decisions
Distinguishes financial impact from impact on people and planet, or describes both lenses
Explains how scale, severity and likelihood are used to judge a topic
Names the subjectivity or tradeoff in deciding what to include
Recognises that omitting unflattering material information risks greenwashing

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining and justifying a materiality judgment to others, which no listed mission or engine practises directly.

lessons.plain: A Sustainability Management Plan is the document that says how a project will handle its effects on people, money and the environment. This objective is about checking whether a specific plan does two things well: whether it has real safeguards against bribery, meaning offering or taking improper payments or favours to win business or influence decisions, and whether it builds lasting benefit for the local community rather than a token gesture. You are given a scenario and must spot what is missing, weak, or aimed at the wrong people, then say which standard or control would fix it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A contractor on your project offers the local official who approves permits a 'consulting fee' paid to a relative's company. Before reading further, what would a sound plan need to include to stop this, and who should own that control?
lessons.teach:
Anti-bribery means preventing anyone acting for the project from offering, promising, giving, asking for or accepting something of value to improperly influence a decision. Something of value covers cash, gifts, hospitality, jobs, sponsorships and payments routed through relatives or shell companies. A third party is any outside person or firm acting for the project, such as a supplier, agent or consultant. Due diligence means checking a third party's ownership, reputation and track record before engaging it. A facilitation payment is a small payment to speed up a routine action; many organisations ban these outright, so a plan must say whether they are allowed. Community development, often called social responsibility, means the project leaves local people better off through local hiring, fair benefit-sharing, and a grievance channel where complaints are logged and answered.

Why it works: bribery risk sits where money meets decisions. A good plan maps those points, assigns an owner, and attaches a control to each: due diligence before hiring an agent, a gifts-and-hospitality register with approval limits, training, and a confidential reporting route. Monitoring and periodic review show whether the controls still work.

Worked example: a plan says 'We will train staff on anti-bribery.' Trace it. Who is trained? When? Does it cover contractors and agents? Is there evidence the training happened? A stronger version names the third parties in scope, requires signed declarations, sets a gifts threshold, and records approvals. Each question moves the plan from a statement of intent to a checkable control.

Common mistake: treating a policy document as a control. A policy nobody checks does not stop a payment routed through a cousin's company.

Consequence: without third-party screening, the first sign of trouble may be an audit finding or a regulator's inquiry, and the project can lose its permits and its funding.

questions.prompt: A rail-equipment maker in a regional tender hires a local customs broker, Dalton Freight, to clear its shipments through port. The plan's steps so far are: (1) name Dalton Freight as a third party in scope, since it acts for the project; (2) name the logistics manager as the owner of the broker relationship; (3) require due diligence on Dalton's ownership, reputation and track record before the contract is signed. The one step not yet written is this: the plan must state whether the broker may make facilitation payments, which are small payments to speed up routine port actions. Which sentence completes the plan correctly?
choices: Dalton Freight may raise its fee to secure faster clearance, and the cost will be recorded as a logistics expense.
The plan must state explicitly whether facilitation payments are allowed for Dalton Freight, since many organisations ban them outright and the plan has to say which rule applies.
Dalton Freight's ownership claim may be accepted without checking, because it is a small local firm.
Port staff alone will receive anti-bribery training, with the completion date recorded in the training file.
questions.why: A facilitation payment is a small payment to speed a routine action, and because many organisations ban these, the plan has to state whether they are allowed for the broker.

questions.prompt: During a tender that a consultant is advising on, the consultant offers the project's site manager a paid weekend stay at a supplier's resort. Using the anti-bribery definition, what makes this a concern?
choices: The consultant is not a supplier, so the stay cannot be used to influence the tender.
The concern only arises if the site manager personally signs the contract award.
Hospitality is something of value, and offering it to influence a decision during a tender is what the rule prevents.
Only cash counts as something of value, so a weekend stay falls outside the anti-bribery rule.
questions.why: Hospitality counts as something of value, and the rule targets offering anything of value to improperly influence a decision, which a tender decision would be.

questions.prompt: A water utility's plan says community complaints are collected in a box at the village office and tallied once a month, but no complaint is logged with a date, and no reply is sent. Which statement best identifies the gap?
choices: The plan has a suggestion box but not a grievance channel, because complaints are neither logged nor answered.
The plan is compliant, because the channel exists and is reviewed every month.
The box should be replaced by a fair benefit-sharing scheme, which is a separate control.
The monthly tally is too frequent, and complaints should be collected annually instead.
questions.why: A grievance channel must log complaints and answer them, and the described process does neither, so it fails the community development requirement.

questions.prompt: A regional water project proposes engaging a local agent to secure permit approvals. The agent was introduced by a senior official's relative and has no recorded track record. Under the plan's controls, what must happen first?
choices: Add the agent's fees to the gifts-and-hospitality register so the approvals are recorded.
Train the agent on anti-bribery after the contract is signed, so the training covers the work.
Run due diligence on the agent's ownership, reputation and track record before engaging the agent.
Obtain a signed declaration from the agent after the first permit payment is made.
questions.why: Due diligence checks a third party's ownership, reputation and track record before engagement, and this agent has an unverified background and a link to an official, so checking must come first.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would judge whether the anti-bribery and community sections of a Sustainability Management Plan are adequate for a given scenario. Name the specific control you would look for and one limit or tradeoff of relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would check whether each bribery risk point in the scenario has a named owner and a concrete control, not just a policy statement. For third parties, I would look for due diligence before engagement, signed anti-bribery declarations, and audit rights in the contract. I would check the gifts and hospitality rules for thresholds and a register, and whether facilitation payments are banned. For community development, I would look for a grievance mechanism with logged, answered complaints, local hiring targets, and benefit-sharing agreed with the community. The limit is that a control can exist on paper while nobody runs it, so I would ask for evidence such as completed checks and training records. The tradeoff is that thorough due diligence slows procurement, so I would focus it first on the highest-risk third parties.
rubricPoints: Names a concrete control, such as third-party due diligence or a gifts register, rather than a general policy
Assigns ownership and asks for evidence that the control operates
Covers community development through grievance handling, local benefit, or stakeholder agreement
States a real limit or tradeoff, such as paper controls or slower procurement

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style scenario to choose the right control adds the most here, and no listed mission or engine covers reviewing an anti-bribery plan.

lessons.plain: When a project commits to sustainability goals, such as cutting energy use, reducing emissions, or making sure suppliers treat workers fairly, someone has to make those goals happen day to day. This lesson is about who does what. The project manager runs the work: turning the plan into tasks, tracking results, and raising problems. The sponsor is the senior leader who owns the business case and makes calls the project cannot make alone. The PMO, or project management office, sets common methods and looks across many projects. Systems thinking means remembering that a change in one part of the project ripples into others, so the manager looks at connections, not just one task at a time.
lessons.guessPrompt: On a project with a sustainability plan, who should decide whether to accept a higher cost to hit an environmental target: the project manager, the sponsor, or the PMO? Give your best guess and a reason.
lessons.teach:
A Sustainability Management Plan, or SMP, is the document that states how a project will meet its sustainability commitments, such as energy, emissions, waste, labour, and community goals. Writing the plan is one job; carrying it out is another, and authority is split between three roles.

The project manager (PM) is accountable for implementing the SMP inside the project. That means building its actions into the schedule and budget, assigning owners, tracking the agreed metrics, managing the risks that could derail them, and reporting progress. The PM can make decisions within the project's approved scope and tolerances, which are the limits the sponsor has set for cost, time, and scope. The PM cannot change the business case on their own.

The sponsor is the senior executive who owns the business case, funds the project, and holds authority the PM lacks. Any decision that trades a sustainability target against cost or schedule beyond the agreed tolerances goes to the sponsor. The PMO, the project management office, sets standard templates, methods, and governance checkpoints, and compares performance across projects.

Systems thinking means treating the project as part of a larger system with feedback loops and delayed effects. A cheaper material may cut cost now but raise emissions later in the supply chain, so a good PM traces those knock-on effects before acting.

Worked example: a PM finds that a supplier change would cut waste by 15 percent but add two weeks. Step one, the PM checks the change against the schedule tolerance, which is exceeded. Step two, the PM documents the trade-off and its effect on the SMP metrics. Step three, the PM escalates to the sponsor, who decides. Step four, the PMO records the decision in the governance log.

Common mistake: the PM quietly accepts the trade-off to avoid a difficult conversation, or the sponsor delegates the sustainability target entirely and never reviews it. The consequence is that SMP metrics drift, and the organisation later cannot show that it kept its commitments.

The PM implements, the sponsor decides anything beyond tolerance, and the PMO keeps the standard consistent.

questions.prompt: A project manager is delivering a fleet of 40 electric delivery vans for a regional bakery chain. The SMP commits to cutting fleet emissions by 25 percent. The project's approved cost tolerance, the overrun limit the sponsor has set, is 20,000 pounds. A battery supplier change would cut lifetime emissions further but add 35,000 pounds. Step one: the PM checks the change against the cost tolerance and finds it exceeded. Step two: the PM documents the trade-off and its effect on the emissions metric in the SMP tracking log. Step three is missing. What comes next?
choices: The PM removes the emissions metric from the SMP so the cost tolerance is no longer exceeded.
The PM approves the supplier change directly, since lower emissions meet the SMP commitment.
The PM escalates the decision to the sponsor, who holds the authority to approve spending beyond tolerance.
The PMO approves the change and the PM updates the schedule afterwards.
questions.why: Any trade-off beyond the agreed tolerance belongs to the sponsor, who owns the business case and funds the project, so the PM escalates rather than deciding alone.

questions.prompt: A packaging redesign at a food company has an SMP target of 40 percent recycled content in its cartons. The PM finds that lowering the target to 30 percent would save six weeks. Who makes this decision?
choices: The PM, because the target is part of the project's day-to-day delivery.
The supplier, because the recycled content is their material.
The PMO, because it sets the standard templates for targets.
The sponsor, because the change trades a sustainability target against schedule beyond tolerance.
questions.why: Trading a sustainability target against schedule beyond the agreed tolerance is a sponsor decision, not one the PM or PMO can make alone.

questions.prompt: A construction firm's project team switches to a cheaper paint that saves money in the first year. Later, the paint needs repainting twice as often, increasing solvent waste and transport trips. Which action best reflects systems thinking by the project manager?
choices: Trace the delayed knock-on effects of the change, such as repainting waste and transport, before accepting it.
Assume the supplier will report any later environmental problems.
Wait until the waste figures appear in the final project report.
Track only the first-year cost, since the saving is what the sponsor approved.
questions.why: Systems thinking means following feedback loops and delayed effects, such as later waste and transport, before the change is accepted.

questions.prompt: A regional building firm runs five separate projects, and each project tracks waste with a different method, so the firm cannot compare results. Which role is responsible for setting a consistent standard across these projects?
choices: The PMO, which sets standard templates and methods and compares performance across projects.
The project manager of each project, who tracks the agreed metrics.
The sponsor of each project, who owns the business case for that project.
The site contractor, who records the waste generated on the ground.
questions.why: The PMO sets standard templates, methods, and governance checkpoints and compares performance across projects, so it keeps the measurement standard consistent.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says the project manager should decide whether to accept a sustainability trade-off that adds cost, since the PM runs the project day to day. Explain to them who should decide, where the project manager's role stops, and one limit of your own answer.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would say the project manager should not make that call alone. The PM owns implementation: scheduling the SMP actions, assigning owners, tracking metrics, and reporting. That authority covers choices within the approved tolerances for cost, time, and scope. A trade-off that adds cost beyond those tolerances changes the business case, and the sponsor owns that case and holds the funding. So the PM documents the impact on the sustainability metrics, escalates, and the sponsor decides. The PMO then records the decision so it is consistent with other projects. One limit of this answer is that tolerances differ between organisations, so the exact boundary depends on what the sponsor has approved in the project's governance documents.
rubricPoints: The project manager implements the SMP and decides only within approved tolerances.
The sponsor owns the business case and decides trade-offs that exceed those tolerances.
The PMO sets standards, templates, and governance records across projects.
Systems thinking means tracing knock-on effects of a change across the wider system.
A good answer names a limit, such as tolerances varying by organisation or the need to check governance documents.

suggested.rationale: Distinguishing PM, sponsor, and PMO authority and explaining it to a teammate is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it.

lessons.plain: A sustainability impact threshold is a line you set in advance that tells you when an environmental or social effect becomes big enough to need action, reporting, or a formal decision. Think of a fuel gauge with a reserve mark: nothing changes until the needle crosses it, and then you act. Project managers use thresholds to decide which impacts are minor, which need a plan, and which could bring legal or contractual consequences. The difficulty is that impacts do not stay inside the project's own walls. A supplier's emissions or a subcontractor's labor practices can matter as much as your own. This lesson covers how to set those lines for an organization, how to look along the whole chain of supply, and what happens when a line is crossed under the rules that apply.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project's own office uses little electricity, but its main materials supplier runs a large, energy-hungry factory. Which of the two should trigger a sustainability review, and why might a rule that only looks at your own building miss the bigger problem?
lessons.teach:
An organizational threshold is a limit the organization sets in advance, such as a maximum amount of emissions, waste, or water use, that switches on a required response when it is crossed. A value-chain impact is an effect that happens across the wider chain of materials, suppliers, transport, customers and disposal, not only inside the organization's own sites. A regulatory compliance consequence is what follows, legally or contractually, when a limit written into law, a permit or a contract is exceeded. Examples include a fine, a suspended permit, or a breached contract clause. Thresholds work because they turn a vague concern into a trigger that someone must act on, and they make decisions repeatable from one review to the next.

Worked example, with illustrative numbers. A road project sets an organizational threshold of 50 tonnes of CO2-equivalent for any single work package, which triggers a formal review. Step 1: estimate the site's own diesel use at 40 tonnes. Step 2: estimate the emissions from the asphalt supplier's production, which is a value-chain impact, at 35 tonnes. Step 3: add them to get 75 tonnes, which exceeds the 50-tonne line. Step 4: check the local permit, which caps the package at 60 tonnes, so 75 is also a compliance breach, not only an internal review.

Common mistake: counting only direct site emissions, so the threshold never fires and the supplier's share goes unseen. Consequence in a running project: the team reports a clean figure, the permit inspector later finds the supplier share, and the work stops until the permit is revised or the supply is changed.

questions.prompt: A bottling plant sets an organizational threshold of 200 cubic metres of water per month for its site, which triggers a formal review. Its permit caps site water abstraction at 250 cubic metres per month. Step 1: the site uses 130 cubic metres this month. Step 2: the glass-bottle supplier's water use, a value-chain impact, is 90 cubic metres. Step 3: the total is 220 cubic metres, which exceeds the 200-cubic-metre organizational threshold. Step 4 is missing. What should the team do next?
choices: Compare the 220-cubic-metre total with the 250-cubic-metre permit cap, find it is under the cap, and conclude there is no compliance breach but the internal review still applies.
Treat the 220 cubic metres as a permit breach, because any total above the internal threshold is automatically illegal.
Report only the 130 cubic metres, because the permit covers only water the site itself abstracts.
Cancel the internal review, because the threshold only matters once a permit is breached.
questions.why: The organizational threshold triggers an internal review, while the permit cap decides whether a legal breach has occurred, and 220 is below 250, so only the review applies.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes a value-chain impact as the term is used in sustainability management planning?
choices: An effect that happens across materials, suppliers, transport, customers and disposal, not only inside the organization's own sites.
Any cost the organization pays to its own staff for training on emissions reporting.
A limit the organization sets in advance that triggers a required response when crossed.
A fine issued by a regulator after a permit limit is exceeded.
questions.why: A value-chain impact is defined in the teaching text as an effect that spreads across the wider chain beyond the organization's own sites.

questions.prompt: A cleaning firm's contract with a hospital says wastewater discharge must not exceed 5 litres of a certain chemical per week. In one week the discharge is 6 litres, and the firm's own internal threshold is 8 litres. Which consequence applies?
choices: No consequence, because the internal threshold of 8 litres was not crossed.
A review trigger only, since internal thresholds always override contract terms.
A suspended environmental permit, because the firm's own threshold was not respected.
A breached contract clause, which is a regulatory compliance consequence, even though the internal threshold was not crossed.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a compliance consequence as following when a limit in a law, permit or contract is exceeded, so the 5-litre contract limit being exceeded creates a breach regardless of the internal threshold.

questions.prompt: Why do organizations set thresholds in their sustainability management plans, rather than only reviewing emissions or waste informally?
choices: Thresholds are required by law in every country, so organizations only record them for audits.
Thresholds guarantee that no value-chain impact will ever occur, because suppliers must then stay below the line.
Thresholds turn a vague concern into a trigger someone must act on and make decisions repeatable from one review to the next.
Thresholds remove the need for any measurement, because the limit itself proves the result.
questions.why: The teaching text states that thresholds work by converting a vague concern into an actionable trigger and by making decisions repeatable across reviews.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a supplier's emissions count against our project's sustainability threshold, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first check whether the threshold is written for the project's direct footprint or for the whole package, because that decides the scope. If the threshold covers the package, I would add the supplier's estimated emissions for the materials we buy from them, using the supplier's own data where we have it and a clearly labeled estimate where we do not. Then I would compare the total with the threshold and, separately, with any permit or contract cap, since crossing a legal limit is a different kind of problem from crossing an internal one. The main limit of this approach is data quality: supplier figures are often incomplete or estimated, so the total can be uncertain. I would record the assumptions and the range, so the review decision stays honest about what we do not yet know.
rubricPoints: States that the threshold's scope (direct only or whole value chain) must be checked before counting supplier emissions
Adds value-chain emissions to direct emissions before comparing with the threshold
Distinguishes an internal organizational threshold from a legal or contractual compliance limit
Names a limit such as incomplete or estimated supplier data, and says how to record the uncertainty

suggested.rationale: Deciding whether a value-chain figure crosses a threshold and what compliance follows is an exam-style judgment that benefits from reasoning through a scenario rather than reading definitions alone.

lessons.plain: Buying things for a project means choosing who supplies them and writing down what they must deliver. Sustainability concerns, such as energy use, waste, fair labour and emissions, can be built into that buying process rather than checked at the end. A key performance indicator, or KPI, is a measurable number that shows whether a goal is being met, such as the share of suppliers that report their emissions. This lesson covers three steps: picking suppliers, choosing a contract type that shares risk fairly, and managing the contract so promises are kept after signing.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project buys a large batch of steel. Supplier A is cheapest but never reports its energy use. Supplier B costs 8 percent more and publishes its emissions. Before reading on, which would you pick for a sustainability-minded project, and what one contract term would you add to protect that choice?
lessons.teach: Procurement means obtaining goods or services from outside suppliers. In a sustainability management plan, procurement is where many impacts enter the project, because a supplier's energy use, waste and labour practices become part of your project's footprint. Three terms matter here. A supplier selection criterion is a rule for judging bids beyond price, such as reported emissions or verified waste handling. A contract type sets how cost and risk are shared. A fixed-price contract pays a set amount for a defined result, so the supplier carries most cost risk. A cost-reimbursable contract pays actual allowable costs plus a fee, so the buyer carries more cost risk and needs stronger oversight. A time-and-materials contract pays per hour and per material, which suits work whose scope is unclear. A KPI is a measurable number tied to a goal, such as the percentage of supplier spend covered by emissions reporting. Why it works: after signing, the contract is the main lever the buyer holds, so sustainability terms must be written in as measurable KPIs with a reporting frequency, audit rights and corrective-action steps. Worked example: a road project buys aggregate. Step 1: score bids with weighted criteria, cost 60 percent and verified emissions data 40 percent. Step 2: choose fixed-price for the crushing work, because its scope is well defined. Step 3: add a KPI requiring quarterly emissions reports and a right to audit. Step 4: in month three the reports are late, so the corrective-action clause triggers a written remediation plan. Common mistake: writing a goal such as 'supplier should be green' with no measure, so nobody can tell whether it was met. Consequence: without a measurable KPI and an audit right, a supplier can miss the sustainability target for the whole project, and the buyer has no contractual lever to act.

questions.prompt: A city library is buying 400 refurbished laptops for a digital-inclusion project. The scope is fully defined, so the team chooses a fixed-price contract. Work through the plan: Step 1: score bids with weighted criteria, price 70 percent and verified e-waste take-back certificates 30 percent. Step 2: choose a fixed-price contract, because the laptop specification is fully defined and the supplier carries most cost risk. Step 3: [MISSING]. Step 4: in month two, 12 percent of take-back certificates are absent, so the corrective-action clause triggers a written remediation plan. Which action completes Step 3?
choices: Switch to a cost-reimbursable contract so the library pays actual costs and the supplier has no reason to hold back on take-back
Pay the full fixed price up front so the supplier has funds to arrange take-back before any laptops are delivered
Remove the e-waste criterion from the contract once the bid is awarded, since weighted scoring is only needed before signing
Add a KPI for the percentage of units with a verified take-back certificate, reported monthly, with a right for the library to audit the supplier's records
questions.why: A measurable KPI with a reporting frequency and an audit right is what gives the buyer a contractual lever, which is why the later corrective-action clause can be triggered.

questions.prompt: A water utility hires a contractor to replace corroded pipe sections, but the number of bad sections will not be known until the trenches are opened. Which contract type fits this unclear scope best?
choices: Fixed-price, because the supplier then carries all the risk of unknown defects
Cost-reimbursable with a fee, because the buyer should bear the full cost of every section
Time-and-materials, because it pays per hour and per material, which suits work whose scope is unclear
Fixed-price with a KPI, because a KPI removes the need to match the contract type to the scope
questions.why: Time-and-materials pays per hour and per material, which suits work whose scope is not yet clear, whereas fixed-price needs a well-defined result to price.

questions.prompt: A hotel group's linen supplier contract states that the supplier should reduce its water use. Why does this clause fail as a sustainability term?
choices: It sets a goal with no measure, so nobody can tell whether it was met or trigger any action
It lacks a fee, so the supplier has no incentive to report
Water use is not a legitimate sustainability topic for a supplier contract
Fixed-price contracts cannot include water-related clauses
questions.why: A goal such as reduce water use has no measurable number, reporting frequency or audit right, so the buyer cannot verify it or act on a shortfall.

questions.prompt: A catering company's food supplier reports its emissions once a year, and the contract has no audit right and no corrective-action step. What is the most serious consequence for the catering company?
choices: The supplier's emissions will automatically fall because annual reporting is mandatory
The company must switch to a time-and-materials contract to recover its costs
The company's own emissions are reduced to zero for the period covered by the report
The company cannot verify the figures or require remediation during the contract, so it has no contractual lever to act on a missed target
questions.why: Without an audit right and a corrective-action clause, the buyer cannot check the supplier's figures or force remediation, so it has no contractual lever to act.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between a fixed-price and a cost-reimbursable contract for a supplier whose sustainability performance matters, and name one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking how well defined the work is. If the scope is clear, a fixed-price contract suits it: the supplier carries most cost risk, so they have a reason to control costs, but they may cut corners on sustainability items unless those are written as measured deliverables with reporting. If the scope is still uncertain or the work is exploratory, a cost-reimbursable contract fits better, because the buyer pays actual costs plus a fee and can require detailed cost and emissions data. The tradeoff is that the buyer carries more cost risk and needs stronger oversight, since the supplier has less pressure to be efficient. Either way, I would add measurable sustainability KPIs, a reporting schedule, audit rights and a corrective-action clause, so the contract type does not decide the sustainability outcome on its own.
rubricPoints: Chooses contract type by how well defined the scope is
States that a fixed-price contract shifts most cost risk to the supplier
States that a cost-reimbursable contract shifts cost risk to the buyer and needs stronger oversight
Explains that sustainability terms need measurable KPIs, reporting and audit rights whatever the contract type

suggested.rationale: Choosing a contract type and KPIs for a supplier is a judgement call best practised through an exam-style procurement situation, and no listed mission covers it.

lessons.plain: Sustainability communication is any message a project sends about its environmental, social or governance effects, such as a status note to the team, a briefing for investors, a formal report or a public marketing claim. Each type has a different job. Some build trust by showing what is really happening, some increase transparency by sharing data people can check, and some are meant to persuade. Greenwashing is the problem that appears when a message creates a green impression that the facts do not back up. A project manager needs to know which kind of message is being written, who will read it, and what evidence must sit behind it before it goes out.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project team wants to tell the public that its new building is 'environmentally friendly.' Before reading further, what single question would you ask before that sentence is published, and why would the answer matter?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A sustainability communication is any message that reports or promises something about a project's environmental, social or governance (ESG) effects. ESG covers three areas that investors and regulators examine: environmental impact, social conduct such as safety and fair treatment, and governance, meaning who decides and who is accountable. A stakeholder is anyone affected by or interested in the project, such as a client, regulator, employee or nearby community. An offset is a purchased credit for emissions reduced somewhere else, and it is not the same as cutting your own emissions.

Communications serve different purposes. Internal status updates keep the team aligned. Stakeholder briefings and formal reports give evidence so outsiders can judge for themselves. Marketing claims aim to persuade.

Why it works: trust grows when a message can be checked. A claim that states a measured number, the method used to measure it, and the limits of that number lets a reader test it. Transparency means making that information available, including the unfavourable parts. Greenwashing is a message that creates a green impression the evidence does not support, often through vague words such as eco-friendly or sustainable with no measurement behind them.

Worked example. A project replaces diesel generators at a remote site. The draft says the site is now 'net zero'. Step 1: identify the type, which is a public claim. Step 2: ask what evidence exists. The team has fuel-use logs showing the batteries cut diesel use, but the remaining diesel is covered by purchased offsets. Step 3: rewrite the claim to state the measured fuel reduction, the share still covered by offsets, and the offset standard used. The public statement is now narrower, but a reader can check it.

Common mistake: treating the communication plan as a marketing job and approving wording before the data team has confirmed the numbers.

Consequence: an unsupported claim can be challenged by regulators or investors, forcing a public correction and weakening trust in every later report.

An unsupported green claim costs more than the wording it contains, because it damages the credibility of the whole disclosure record.

questions.prompt: A port authority is dredging a shipping channel. Its draft press release says the dredging has zero impact on seagrass. Worked steps: Step 1, identify the type: this is a public claim, so it needs evidence a reader can check. Step 2, check the evidence: a pre-works survey recorded 2 hectares of seagrass in the channel footprint, and the after-works survey is scheduled for September but has not been done. Step 3 is missing from the worked example. Which action must come before the claim is approved, and what should the rewritten claim say?
choices: The data team confirms the 2-hectare baseline and the pending after-works survey, and the claim is rewritten to state the measured baseline and that monitoring is still due.
The claim is approved now, since the September survey will very likely show no loss, and the word estimated is added.
The press release is published with a footnote saying the survey is due later, and the wording of the headline stays the same.
Marketing replaces zero impact with seagrass-friendly dredging and publishes once legal has read it.
questions.why: The data team must confirm the numbers before approval, and a checkable claim states the measured baseline and the monitoring status, which is the rewrite the teaching text calls for.

questions.prompt: A construction firm says its head office is now carbon neutral because it bought credits equal to its office emissions. Which statement best describes what those credits are?
choices: A cut in the office's own emissions, achieved by switching heating systems.
A purchased credit for emissions reduced somewhere else, which does not cut the office's own emissions.
A donation to the local community that is counted as a social benefit.
A government-issued permit that allows the office to emit a fixed amount each year.
questions.why: An offset is a purchased credit for reductions made elsewhere, so it does not reduce the office's own emissions, which is the distinction the teaching text draws.

questions.prompt: Which of these messages from a river restoration project carries the greenwashing risk the teaching text warns about, and why?
choices: The report compares the energy cut against a named baseline year and lists the units used.
The river works are eco-friendly and sustainable, with no figures or method given for either word.
The pump station's energy use fell 3% by meter reading, and the report gives the meter's margin of error.
An independent auditor sampled 40 readings and the report states the sample size and result.
questions.why: Vague words such as eco-friendly and sustainable with no measurement behind them create a green impression the evidence does not support, which is the defining feature of greenwashing in the teaching text.

questions.prompt: A site manager sends a message each morning telling the crew which access road is closed and which crane is out of service. What type of sustainability-related or project communication is this, and what is its purpose?
choices: A formal stakeholder report, giving evidence so outsiders can judge the project.
An internal status update, which keeps the team aligned on current conditions.
An ESG annual disclosure, filed for investors and regulators.
A marketing claim, aimed at persuading clients to choose the firm.
questions.why: Internal status updates keep the project team aligned, and a daily crew message about closures and equipment is that kind of communication rather than an outward-facing report or claim.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a sustainability communication that builds trust and one that amounts to greenwashing, and name one limit of judging a message only by its wording.
lessons.modelAnswer: A communication builds trust when it states a specific, measured result, explains how it was measured, and admits what is still unresolved. Greenwashing uses broad words like eco-friendly or sustainable to suggest a benefit the evidence does not show. The practical test is whether a reader could check the claim against records. My limit is that wording alone cannot settle this. A carefully worded claim can still mislead by leaving out an important caveat, such as offsets covering most of the remaining emissions. So I would judge a claim by comparing it with the underlying data, and I would ask the data owner to confirm the numbers before publication.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes trust-building claims (specific, measured, checkable) from greenwashing (vague or unsupported impressions)
Names the purpose of at least two communication types, such as internal updates, stakeholder reports and marketing
Explains that transparency includes disclosing caveats and limits, not only favourable results
States a real limit, such as wording that looks precise but omits a material qualification, and says evidence must be checked

suggested.rationale: Explaining the trust-versus-greenwashing distinction back to a teammate, with a limit, is the core skill this objective tests and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: Projects spend money, use materials, change jobs, and affect people and places. ESG stands for environmental, social and governance, the three groups of effects and controls that investors, lenders, regulators and communities often ask about. Sustainability reporting is the regular written account of those effects and how they are managed. Materiality is the test for which effects are important enough to include. A report that lists everything hides the few facts that matter, so choosing what to report is a key step. This lesson links what a project actually does to what gets disclosed, and explains why that selection step matters.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project replaces a diesel generator at a depot with a battery system. Before reading on, which of its effects would you expect to appear in a sustainability report, and which would you leave out? Give a reason for each choice.
lessons.teach:
A project activity is any piece of work that changes something, such as buying equipment, moving materials, hiring, building, or changing a process. An effect is a result of that activity that someone outside the project can notice or measure, such as lower fuel use, more traffic, or changed working hours. ESG stands for environmental, social and governance. An ESG disclosure is a specific statement about one such effect or control, given with a figure or a clear description. A sustainability report gathers those disclosures for a period into one document. Materiality is the test for which disclosures belong in the report: an effect is material when a reasonable reader would be influenced by knowing about it.

The link works because each disclosure should trace back to an activity you can name. If you cannot point to the activity that produced a number, the number is probably not reliable enough to publish.

Worked example. A project replaces gas boilers at a depot with heat pumps. Step one: name the activity, which is removing two boilers and installing pumps. Step two: list the effects. Gas use falls by an estimated 300 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent a year (environmental and measurable). Two weeks of drilling noise affect nearby residents (social and short). A refrigerant charge is added to the system (environmental, and possibly regulated). Step three: apply materiality. The gas reduction is large and central to the project's purpose, so it is material. The refrigerant charge is material if it is a regulated gas. Two weeks of noise is material only if residents complained or the site is sensitive. Step four: disclose the material items and record their source.

Common mistake: publishing every activity, which buries the important facts, or publishing only the flattering effects, which misleads readers and invites greenwashing claims, meaning overstated environmental claims. Consequence in a running system: if the project changes which meters feed the energy data, the reported gas figure can jump with no real change in use, so the reporting team must record the change and its effect on the trend.

Materiality is therefore a judgement you record, not a formula you hide.

questions.prompt: A coffee roaster replaces its old gas roasting oven with a new unit that burns less gas. The project team works through the first three steps. Step one: the activity is removing the old oven and installing the new one. Step two: the effects are an estimated 120 MWh a year less gas use (environmental, measurable), six odour complaints logged from neighbours in the first month (social, and the site is close to homes), and a switch to recyclable bean bags (environmental, minor). Step three: the gas reduction is central to the project's purpose, so it is material. The odour complaints are material because the site is close to homes and the complaints were logged. The bag switch is not material. Step four, which the reporter has not yet done, is the one that makes each published figure checkable by someone else. Which choice describes step four?
choices: Publish every effect, including the bag switch, so readers can judge for themselves.
Record the source of each published figure, such as the metered reading or the stated estimate method, so the number can be traced back to the activity.
Remove the odour complaints from the log so the disclosure reads cleanly and avoids alarming readers.
Publish only the gas reduction, since the neighbour complaints are a local matter outside the report.
questions.why: Step four is recording the source of each material disclosure so that it can be traced to the activity that produced it, which is the requirement the teaching text sets for publishable numbers.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, which statement best defines materiality as used in sustainability reporting?
choices: An effect is material when a reasonable reader would be influenced by knowing about it.
An effect is material when a regulator has already issued a fine for it.
An effect is material when the project team considers it important enough to report to its own managers.
An effect is material when its measured value is larger than the project's budget for that year.
questions.why: Materiality is the test of whether a reasonable reader would be influenced by knowing the effect, not an internal, budget or regulatory threshold.

questions.prompt: A farm's irrigation upgrade cuts water use by 30 percent, which is published in its sustainability report. The monitoring data also shows nitrate runoff into a nearby stream rose by 40 percent over the same period, but that figure is left out. What is the main problem with the report?
choices: The report omits a material effect that cuts against the flattering one, which misleads readers and invites greenwashing claims.
The report should have listed the irrigation activity as an effect rather than a result.
The water figure is too large to be credible, so readers will distrust the whole report.
The runoff figure belongs in a separate governance document, so leaving it out is acceptable.
questions.why: Publishing only the flattering effects while omitting a material negative one misleads readers and exposes the report to overstated environmental claims.

questions.prompt: A council's road-resurfacing project reports that resident commute emissions fell 8 percent this year. The project team cannot identify any activity in the project that would have caused this change, and the figure came from a general regional dataset. What should the reporting lead do?
choices: Hold the figure back from publication until it can be traced to a named project activity.
Split the figure in half and publish one half to be safe.
Publish the figure because a regional dataset is usually more reliable than project records.
Publish the figure with a note that the project is not responsible for it.
questions.why: The teaching rule is that a number you cannot link to the activity that produced it is probably not reliable enough to publish, so it should be held until traced.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says the sustainability report should list every project activity so nothing is hidden. Explain to them how project activities, ESG disclosures and materiality connect, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would explain it as a chain. Each activity produces effects, and each effect that someone outside the project would care about can become a disclosure, which is a stated fact with a figure or description. Materiality is the filter between them: we only publish effects a reasonable reader would be influenced by, such as a large reduction in emissions or a regulated substance added to a site. Listing every activity does not make the report more honest, it makes the important facts harder to find. The tradeoff is that materiality is a judgement, so two reasonable people can disagree. We reduce that risk by writing down why each item was included or left out, and by checking that we are not dropping inconvenient effects, since leaving out the bad news is itself a greenwashing risk.
rubricPoints: Each disclosure traces back to a named project activity and its effect.
Materiality filters which effects are reported, based on what a reasonable reader needs.
Listing everything hides material facts; publishing only positive effects misleads.
