Materiality is a recorded judgement with a stated tradeoff or limit.

suggested.rationale: Connecting activities, disclosures and materiality is best shown by explaining the chain to someone else, and no listed mission or planned engine covers ESG reporting.

lessons.plain: Governance is the set of rules, roles, and decision points that decide who approves what, who checks it, and how problems get escalated on a project. A governance framework is a documented version of those rules, chosen to fit the situation. For sustainability work, it also covers how environmental and social promises are tracked, reviewed, and signed off before they reach the public. Think of it like the house rules for a shared kitchen: not the food itself, but who buys, who cooks, who checks the fridge dates, and what happens when something goes wrong. Choosing a framework means matching the rules to the project's size, risk, and public visibility, rather than copying a template from somewhere else.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small team is running a community recycling pilot and plans to publish a claim that it cut waste by 40 percent. Before reading further, what would you put in place to decide who signs off that claim, and why might one person approving their own work be risky?
lessons.teach:
A governance framework is the agreed structure for decisions on a project: who decides what, who reviews it, what evidence is needed, and where decisions are recorded. Decision rights are the explicit permissions to approve a specific kind of decision. Escalation is the route a problem takes when it exceeds the authority of the person who found it. Assurance means an independent check that a result or claim is supported by evidence.

Good governance has recognisable characteristics. Roles and decision rights are named, not implied. The depth of control is proportionate to risk: a public claim needs more review than an internal note. Decisions and their evidence are documented so someone can trace them later. Review happens at a set point before anything is published or committed. The framework is revisited when the project changes.

Worked example. The pilot team wants to publish the 40 percent claim. Step 1: the data owner prepares the calculation and its source figures. Step 2: because the claim is public, the risk is classed as high. Step 3: an independent reviewer checks the method and the data. Step 4: the sponsor approves publication. Step 5: the decision and reviewer's notes go into the decision log.

Common mistake: the same person prepares, checks, and approves the claim, so no independent check happens. Consequence in a running system: an unchecked figure goes out, is later corrected, and the team loses public trust and must redo its reporting.

A framework that exists only on paper does not protect anyone; it must be followed at the points where decisions are made.

questions.prompt: A housing charity runs a pilot that fitted insulation to 60 flats and wants to claim a heating-cost saving in a grant bid. Step 1: the site coordinator compiles two winters of gas bills for the flats, before and after the work. Step 2: because the figure will go into a funding bid, the risk is classed as high. Step 3: an independent reviewer finds that the baseline winter used a different count of heating days from the after winter, and cannot settle the difference alone. Step 4: [missing]. Step 5: the sponsor's decision and the reviewer's notes go into the decision log before anything is submitted. What belongs in the missing step 4?
choices: The reviewer averages the two winters' heating days, adjusts the baseline, and signs off alone so the bid can go in on time.
The project manager removes the disputed winter from the evidence file so the decision log shows a clean, consistent comparison.
The reviewer escalates the heating-day mismatch to the named sponsor, who holds the decision right over the claim, and the claim is held until the sponsor rules on it.
The coordinator submits the grant bid now and records the heating-day mismatch in an appendix for the funder to examine.
questions.why: When a reviewer finds a problem they cannot resolve within their own authority, the framework routes it upward through escalation to whoever holds the decision right, and the claim waits until that person decides.

questions.prompt: In a project governance framework, what is a decision right?
choices: A general duty for the whole team to keep the project moving and to report problems when they appear.
An explicit permission to approve one specific kind of decision, held by a named role.
The route a problem follows when it goes beyond the authority of the person who found it.
The right of any stakeholder to view the project's cost records and performance dashboards at any time.
questions.why: A decision right is an explicit approval permission attached to a specific kind of decision and a named role; the escalation route and general duties are different concepts.

questions.prompt: A small internal team produces a draft note summarising how much time its staff saved after moving to a new scheduling tool. The note is only for the team's own weekly meeting. Which governance approach best fits this scenario?
choices: Have a single trusted person prepare and approve the note, with light checks proportionate to a low-risk internal use.
Hold the note until an external assurance provider has verified every figure, even though it is never published.
Skip all documentation, because internal notes never need a record anyone could trace later.
Apply the same full review and independent sign-off that a public regulatory claim would need, so the process is identical everywhere.
questions.why: Good governance matches the depth of control to the risk, so an internal, low-risk note needs lighter review than a public claim, though it should still be recorded sensibly.

questions.prompt: A project team has a written governance framework that names decision owners and review points. During a busy launch week, the team skips the review point and publishes a figure anyway. Which statement best describes what has gone wrong?
choices: The framework has failed its purpose, because a framework that exists only on paper does not protect anyone and must be followed at the points where decisions are made.
The framework is still valid, because the written document names the reviewers and so the review has effectively happened.
The framework should be deleted, because a skipped review proves that rigid structures slow projects too much.
The team should move the review to after publication, since a later correction is always cheaper than a delay.
questions.why: A framework only protects the project when it is followed at the actual decision points; a named but skipped review point leaves the figure unchecked despite the document existing.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose a governance framework for a sustainability project that will publish a public emissions claim. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by classing the project's risk. A public emissions claim is high risk, so it needs more structure than an internal update. I would name a data owner who prepares the figures, an independent reviewer who checks the method and source data, and a sponsor who approves publication. Each decision would be recorded with its evidence in a decision log, so we can trace it later. The main tradeoff is speed: independent review adds time before publication, and if the review stage is rushed or skipped, the framework gives false confidence. For a small pilot I would keep the same roles but scale the review depth down, and I would revisit the framework if the project grows or the claim's audience widens.
rubricPoints: Matches the depth of governance to the risk and public visibility of the claim
Names distinct roles for preparing, independently reviewing, and approving the decision
Requires decisions and evidence to be documented and traceable
States a concrete limit or tradeoff, such as added time or false confidence if review is weak
Notes that the framework should be revisited as the project changes

suggested.rationale: Justifying a governance structure out loud is the core skill here, and no listed mission covers this objective.

scenarios.title: Flood-Zone Roastery at Brightwater Coffee Roasters
scenarios.scenario: Brightwater Coffee Roasters is a fictional mid-sized company that buys green coffee beans from smallholder farms and roasts them in its own facility. The company plans to build a new roastery on a low-lying coastal site. Before the board approves funding, the project sponsor, Maya, asks you to prepare the sustainability case. Sustainability here means meeting today's needs without harming the ability of future people and ecosystems to meet theirs. The project team has three open questions. The site is in a area that regional maps show could flood more often as sea levels rise, so the design must keep working during and after flooding. The company's buyers in Europe have asked for climate disclosures, and the finance team wants to know which reporting standard to follow. The board also wants the project tied to recognized global goals so that it can be explained to investors and local partners. Please answer the following: 1. Name the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) that this project most directly supports or puts at risk, and explain how the UN Global Compact principles apply to the way the company treats its workers and its suppliers. 2. Explain the Triple Bottom Line (a way of judging a project on People, Planet, and Prosperity together) for this roastery, giving one specific consideration under each heading. 3. Recommend which disclosure framework the finance team should use for climate-related financial risk, and explain how a general ESG disclosure differs from that framework. 4. Distinguish resilience from regeneration (the idea of leaving a place or system better than you found it), and state which of these the flood-zone design aims for and which the supplier farm programme aims for.
subParts: SDGs and UN Global Compact principles
Climate disclosure framework and how ESG disclosure differs
modelAnswer: The most direct links are SDG 13 (Climate Action), because the project sits in a flood-prone zone and its emissions from roasting add to climate change; SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure), because building resilient infrastructure and upgrading processes is the core of the work; and SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth), because the roastery will employ people and the supplier programme affects farm incomes. SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation) is relevant if wastewater from roasting or washing is discharged near the site. The UN Global Compact is a voluntary set of ten principles covering human rights, labour, the environment, and anti-corruption that companies commit to following in their operations and supply chains. For Brightwater, the labour principles mean fair pay and safe working conditions in the new roastery, and the human rights and labour principles extend to checking that supplier farms do not use child or forced labour. A common mistake is to pick every SDG that sounds good; a strong answer names only the goals the project actually affects and gives a reason for each.

The People heading covers effects on workers, neighbours, and communities. For example, the project should plan safe access routes and emergency shelter for staff during floods, and it should consider whether local residents will be affected by traffic or noise during construction. The Planet heading covers environmental effects such as energy use, emissions, water use, and waste. For example, the roastery's gas-fired roasters will produce carbon emissions, so the team should estimate them and look at electric or heat-recovery options. The Prosperity heading covers economic value, including whether the project produces a return the company can sustain and whether it supports local supply chains. For example, paying farmers a fair price and building a long-term supply relationship may cost more upfront but reduces the risk of supply disruption. The key idea is that the three headings are weighed together rather than one being treated as an afterthought. A common mistake is to list only financial benefits and call the project sustainable; a good answer gives at least one specific point under each heading.

The finance team should use the TCFD-aligned climate standard, now maintained by the International Sustainability Standards Board as IFRS S2 (Climate-related Disclosures). TCFD stands for the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures, a framework that asks companies to report how climate change creates financial risks and opportunities across four areas: governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets. This fits the flood-zone question because it asks how physical flood risk could affect the value of the asset and the company's cash flows. A general ESG disclosure, by contrast, is a broad report on environmental, social, and governance performance, often covering many topics and written for a range of stakeholders. ESG is an umbrella term rather than a single standard. GRI (Global Reporting Initiative) standards focus on the impacts the company has on people and the environment, while SASB (Sustainability Accounting Standards Board) standards focus on industry-specific sustainability issues that could affect financial performance and are aimed mainly at investors. A common mistake is to treat ESG, GRI, SASB, and TCFD as interchangeable; a strong answer explains that the first is a broad concept and the others are specific frameworks with different audiences and aims.

Resilience is the ability of a project or system to withstand an extreme event, or to recover from it quickly, while still doing its job. Regeneration goes further: it aims to restore or improve the natural or social systems the project touches, so that the net effect is positive over time. The flood-zone design is about resilience. Examples include raising the building floor above the expected flood level, placing electrical equipment on upper floors, and designing drainage that can handle heavy rain. The supplier farm programme is closer to regeneration. For example, if the company funds shade-tree planting and soil restoration on partner farms, the farms may end up healthier and more productive than before, which goes beyond simply avoiding harm. A common mistake is to call flood defences regenerative because they are good for the environment; they protect the asset but do not necessarily restore the ecosystem, so resilience is the more accurate label.

scenarios.title: Dye-recycling plant planning at Harrow Vale Textiles
scenarios.scenario: Harrow Vale Textiles Ltd is a fictional mid-sized clothing maker that is starting a project to build a wastewater dye-recycling unit at its single factory. The project is now in the planning stage of a PRiSM (Projects Integrating Sustainable Methods) life cycle. PRiSM is a framework that adds sustainability thinking on top of ordinary project management, so the project is judged not only on time, cost and scope but also on its effects on people, planet, profit, process and product, which is often called the P5 view. Priya Nair is the newly appointed project manager. She moves here from a conventional construction background and works with a sponsor, a finance lead, a community liaison and a procurement officer. The sponsor wants a clear plan before the planning stage closes. Answer the three numbered items below. 1. Name the main planning-stage deliverable that records how the project will manage its People, Planet, Profit, Process and Product effects, and say what decision it lets the team make. 2. The community liaison wants nearby residents involved before the design is locked. Name the supporting process that covers this and describe one practice she should use. 3. The procurement officer proposes buying the filter membranes from the cheapest supplier. Name the supporting process that governs this choice and state one sustainability criterion Priya should add to the decision.
subParts: Planning deliverable for P5 effects and the decision it supports
Supporting process for residents and one practice to use
Supporting process governing the membrane purchase and one added criterion
modelAnswer: The main deliverable is the Sustainability Management Plan. It is the planning-stage document that records how the project will manage its effects on People (workers and nearby communities), Planet (water, air, materials and habitats), Profit (money and value), Process (how the work is done) and Product (what is delivered and how it is used over its life). It draws on the P5 impact analysis, which is a structured look at those effects that is started early and refined during planning. The decision it supports is which design options and trade-offs to accept before the budget and schedule are fixed. Common mistake: treating it as a closing report written after the design is frozen. Consequence: if effects are only recorded after the design is locked, changing the design later costs far more.

The supporting process is stakeholder engagement. A stakeholder is any person or group who is affected by the project or can influence it, such as residents, workers, regulators and suppliers. Stakeholder engagement is the set of practices for identifying these groups, understanding their concerns and involving them in decisions. A practical practice for the liaison is to build a stakeholder map that lists each group and its interest, then hold a structured consultation session with residents early in planning. She should record each concern in a log, respond to it in writing, and show where it changed the design, for example by adjusting the wastewater discharge limit or the noise schedule for the unit. Common mistake: holding one information briefing and calling it consultation. Consequence: unaddressed concerns often return as objections or delays once construction starts.

The governing process is sustainable procurement. Procurement means obtaining goods or services through a formal buying process, and sustainable procurement adds environmental, social and lifecycle criteria to the normal price and quality checks. Priya should keep price as one criterion but not the only one. A suitable added criterion is the supplier's evidence of the membrane's lifecycle impact, such as its energy use in manufacture, its chemical content, or whether it can be recycled or replaced rather than discarded. A supplier with a recognised environmental certification or a stated end-of-life take-back scheme would score higher on this criterion. Common mistake: choosing the lowest bid without checking whether the membrane will last or what it contains. Consequence: a cheap membrane that fails early or contains restricted chemicals can cause repeated replacement, extra waste and a breach of discharge limits in the running plant.

scenarios.title: Halden Bottling Refill Line: P5 Impact Analysis at Closure
scenarios.scenario:
Halden Bottling Co. is a fictional mid-sized drinks company in a coastal town. Its project, called Refill Line, installed a machine that washes and refills returnable glass bottles in place of single-use plastic bottles. The project manager, Priya, is preparing the P5 Impact Analysis before the project closes. P5 is a five-part sustainability lens with the parts Product (what is made and how long it lasts), Process (how work is done and how well), People (workers, communities, customers, and ethics), Planet (the natural environment and resource use), and Prosperity (money, business value, and economic effects). A P5 Impact Analysis lists each change the project causes and sorts each one under the right P. A P5 item is material when it is important enough that a reasonable stakeholder would expect it to influence a decision or appear in a public report. Priya has collected these notes: (a) the new washer uses about 40 percent less water per bottle than the old line; (b) the glass bottles are designed to be refilled roughly 30 times before retirement; (c) bottling shifts are staffed by an outside agency whose workers are paid below the local minimum wage; (d) the machine's maintenance plan needs a replacement valve shipped from overseas every six months; (e) the marketing team's draft brochure calls the line 'zero-waste bottling'. Complete the following tasks.

1. Assign items (a), (b) and (c) each to one P and name the subcategory or element it belongs to. Explain in one sentence why each one fits where you placed it.

2. Item (d) concerns servicing. Name the product lens that covers it, state what Priya should record about the valve supply, and explain why a supply-chain fact belongs in a lifespan or servicing review rather than being ignored.

3. Evaluate item (e). Decide whether it creates an ethics risk under the People lens, explain what the risk is in plain terms, and state one change Priya should request before the brochure is published.

4. At closure, Priya must decide whether item (c) is material for the public sustainability report. Give your decision, justify it using the materiality definition, and describe what the report entry should say about the agency workers.
subParts: Assign items (a), (b), (c) to P5 categories and elements with a one-sentence reason each
Identify the product lens for item (d) and what to record about the valve supply
Evaluate item (e) for greenwashing or ethics risk and propose one change
Decide whether item (c) is material for the public report and describe the report entry
modelAnswer: Item (a) belongs under Planet, in the natural resources or water-use subcategory, because it changes how much water the process consumes per unit made. Item (b) belongs under Product, in the lifespan element, because it describes how many uses a product is designed to survive before it is retired. Item (c) belongs under People, in the labor practices and decent work element, because it concerns the pay and conditions of the people doing the work. A strong answer names all three correctly and gives a reason tied to what each change affects.

Item (d) falls under the Product lens, specifically servicing, because it concerns how the product is kept running and what parts maintenance requires. Priya should record the valve's source country, the shipping frequency (every six months), the lead time if a shipment is late, and the effect on the machine if the valve is unavailable. This belongs in a servicing review because a part that is hard to get can shorten the working life of the line or cause downtime, which changes both lifespan and the cost of keeping the product in service. Ignoring it would leave a known risk out of the impact picture. A strong answer names the Product lens and servicing, lists at least two facts to record, and links the supply fact to lifespan or downtime.

Item (e) creates a greenwashing risk, meaning a claim that makes a project or product sound more environmentally sound than the evidence supports. The line reduces single-use plastic and uses less water, but it is not zero waste: washing, transport and eventual bottle retirement still produce waste, and the overseas valve adds its own impact. Because the claim is misleading to customers, it is an ethics problem under the People lens, which covers honest dealings with customers and anti-corruption as well as greenwashing. Priya should request a change such as replacing 'zero-waste' with a specific, measured claim like 'reduces single-use plastic bottles' and attaching the measured figures. A strong answer identifies the claim as overstated, explains why it misleads, and proposes a specific, evidence-based wording change.

Yes, item (c) is material. Under the materiality definition, a reasonable stakeholder such as an investor, customer, regulator or worker advocate would expect to know that a major operational part of the project depends on workers paid below the local minimum wage, and this could influence how they judge the company. The report entry should state plainly that bottling shifts are staffed through an outside agency, that some workers were paid below the local minimum wage during the project, the date the issue was identified, and the corrective action being taken, such as back pay, a change of agency, or direct hiring. It should not hide the issue behind general wording about commitment to fair work. A strong answer gives a clear yes or no, justifies it with the materiality test, and describes a factual, specific report entry.

scenarios.title: Northmere pump station upgrade: integrity, threshold and supplier decisions
scenarios.scenario: Northmere Civil Works Ltd is a fictional mid-sized contractor. Its project manager, Dana Okafor, is six months into a 14-month upgrade of a regional water pump station for a municipal client. The project has a Sustainability Management Plan, which is a written plan that sets out how the project will manage its environmental, social and governance effects, and it is built on a chosen set of sustainability standards (recognised rule sets that define good practice). The project sponsor, the senior executive who is accountable for the project and funds it, approved the plan. A project management office, or PMO, which is the team that keeps shared project methods, templates and portfolio reports, owns the company's standard forms. Three things have come up in the last two weeks. First, a local agent offered to help secure a planning permit in exchange for a consulting fee paid to a personal account, and a site engineer forwarded the offer. Second, the lead supplier for steel pipework has an emissions estimate for its value chain (the full chain of suppliers and activities feeding the project, upstream and downstream) that, if confirmed, would take Northmere above an organisational reporting threshold, which is a fixed level that triggers extra disclosure duties. Third, procurement is choosing between a fixed-price and a cost-reimbursable contract for the pipework, and the supplier has proposed a key performance indicator, or KPI, which is a measurable target used to track progress. Dana must respond to the following: 1. Name the anti-bribery issue raised by the agent's offer, state what the plan should require in response, and name one community or social-responsibility commitment the plan could add to support the local area. 2. For each of these tasks, state whether the project manager, the sponsor or the PMO should own it: approving an exception to the gift-or-fee policy, updating the shared emissions tracking template, and escalating the threshold question to the company board. 3. State whether the emissions estimate, if confirmed, creates a regulatory consequence, what the threshold decision is, and what could happen to Northmere if it reports the figure incorrectly. 4. Recommend a contract type for the pipework supplier, define one supplier KPI, and name one contract management action that tracks that KPI.
subParts: Anti-bribery issue, required response and one community commitment
Ownership of exception approval, template update and board escalation
Threshold decision and consequence of incorrect reporting
Contract type, supplier KPI and contract management action
modelAnswer: The offer is a bribe, even though it is described as a consulting fee. Paying money to a personal account to influence a permit decision is an improper payment that anti-bribery standards prohibit regardless of the label. The plan should require the offer to be refused, recorded in an integrity or gifts-and-hospitality log, reported to the compliance function and the sponsor, and no agent should be paid until due diligence (checks on who the agent is and what they do) and a written contract with audit rights are in place. A suitable community commitment is a local training or apprenticeship placement for residents near the site, with a measurable target such as a set number of placements per year, which supports social responsibility and gives the community a visible benefit. Consequence: one improper payment can void the permit, expose the company to prosecution and damage trust with the client and the community.

The sponsor should own approving any exception to the gift-or-fee policy, because policy exceptions are a decision-making authority that should sit above the person delivering the work and who is accountable for the project's success. The PMO should own the update to the shared emissions tracking template, since it maintains the standard form used across projects, while the project manager supplies the project data and ensures the updated form is used on site. The sponsor should own escalating the threshold question to the board, with the project manager providing the evidence and the calculations. A common mistake is giving the project manager sole authority over the policy exception, which mixes delivery with control and leaves no independent check.

The estimate creates a regulatory consequence only if it is confirmed. If the verified figure is above the organisational threshold, Northmere takes on a reporting duty and must disclose the value-chain emissions under the applicable rules. The threshold decision is therefore not made on the supplier's unverified estimate alone: the company should check the figure with the supplier's source data and a second calculation, then decide and record the outcome. The common mistake is reporting a lower figure to avoid the trigger, or reporting before verification. Consequence of incorrect reporting: a misstatement can lead to fines, a forced restatement of published figures, loss of client confidence and delays to permits or payments on a live project, because clients and regulators often tie approvals to reporting accuracy.

A fixed-price contract suits the pipework because the scope is well defined, and it moves most cost risk to the supplier. A cost-reimbursable contract would leave Northmere carrying the cost risk and would need tighter audit to control spending. The supplier KPI could be the percentage of pipework batches delivered with a verified low-emission steel certificate issued by an independent mill or testing body, with a target of 100 percent. The contract management action is a monthly review in which the project manager or procurement lead compares certificates received against delivery records, withholds part of the payment for any batch without a valid certificate, and uses the contract's audit right to inspect the supplier's records if the KPI falls below target.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Foods: Cold-Storage Centre Sustainability Claims
scenarios.scenario: Brightwater Foods is a fictional mid-sized packaged-food company building a new cold-storage distribution centre in the town of Eastmere. The project manager, Dana Okafor, leads a team that has drafted a public website post and an input for the quarterly sustainability update. ESG means environmental, social and governance, the three areas companies use to describe how their activities affect people, the planet and how they are run. The draft post says the centre is 'fully green' and will 'cut our footprint to zero'. Internal engineering notes show the centre will rely on diesel backup generators for most of its emergency power, and the carbon offset purchase covers only the first two years of operation. Site staff collect the project's ESG data in spreadsheets, and the steering committee has no written rule on who must approve public sustainability claims. The board has asked Dana to answer three questions. 1. Classify the draft post by its purpose (building trust, increasing transparency, or avoiding greenwashing, where greenwashing means making environmental claims that the facts do not support), name the purpose it fails, and suggest the wording change that fixes it. 2. Explain how the centre's construction and operating activities connect to the ESG disclosures in Brightwater's annual report, and name two reporting topics that are material, where material means significant enough that a reasonable stakeholder would expect them to shape decisions. 3. Propose the characteristics the approval process for public sustainability claims needs, and say who should hold each approval step.
subParts: Classify the draft post and fix the claim
Link project activities to ESG disclosures and materiality
Propose governance for approving sustainability claims
modelAnswer: The post fails the avoiding greenwashing purpose. Its claim of fully green and zero footprint is not supported by the facts: the diesel backup generators produce emissions, and the offset covers only two years. Greenwashing is an overstated environmental claim that the evidence does not back up. A worked check: take each claim, find the evidence, and see if the evidence matches. 'Fully green' fails because the generators are fossil-fuel based; 'zero footprint' fails because the offset ends after two years. The fix is to replace absolute wording with measured, dated, bounded statements, for example 'the centre is designed to run on renewable grid power for daytime operations, with diesel backup used only during outages, and emissions are reported annually against a baseline.' This keeps the trust-building and transparency purposes intact. The common mistake is to soften the wording but keep the claim's meaning, which still misleads. The consequence is that a public overstatement can be challenged by regulators, customers or journalists and damage the company's credibility for years.

Construction and operating activities create the data behind ESG disclosures. Concrete pouring and steel delivery create supply-chain and waste records; the generators and cold-storage refrigeration create energy and emissions records; hiring and local contracting create social records; the approval steps create governance records. Each activity produces evidence, and the annual report must describe that evidence accurately. Materiality is the filter: a topic is material when a reasonable stakeholder such as an investor, lender or local resident would expect it to influence decisions. Two likely material topics for this project are energy and greenhouse gas emissions, because refrigeration and backup generators are large and the project is a long-term asset, and waste or hazardous materials from construction, because local residents and regulators watch them closely. Worked trace: the generators produce emissions, emissions are significant for the centre's footprint, so they go into the disclosure. The mistake is to report only the topics that look good, leaving out the material ones. The consequence is that an omitted material emissions figure makes the whole report misleading when the gap is discovered.

Good governance for claims approval has a few characteristics: clear accountability (one named person owns each decision), independence (the person checking the evidence is not the person who gains from the claim), documented criteria (written standards for what evidence is needed), traceability (a record of who approved what, when, and on what evidence), and proportionality (more scrutiny for public claims than internal notes). A sensible structure is: the site team owns the data and prepares the evidence file; the project manager Dana Okafor owns the draft claim and its accuracy; an independent sustainability or compliance reviewer checks the evidence against the written criteria; and the steering committee gives final sign-off for any public statement and receives a summary each quarter. The common mistake is to let the same person draft, check and approve a claim, which removes the independent check. The consequence is that no one is positioned to catch an overstatement before it is published, so the company carries the reputational and regulatory risk alone.
